speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance and it arises out of continuing uncertainty about the termination of wage and price controls in Canada. Specifically, I should like to ask the Minister of Finance for the validity or the nature of the documents that have been reported on this weekend that suggest that the control program is to end on October 14. What is the nature of those documents, are they official documents, and can we believe what they say?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM POSSIBILITY OF PROGRAM ENDING ON OCTOBER 14 AND THAT RATE OF INFLATION REDUCED TO FOUR PER CENT BY JANUARY,
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated previously to the House and outside the House, we now have under way a process of discussion with the provincial governments and with other major economic decision makers on a possible date for the termination of the controls. I should say that, more than a possible date, it is a range of dates and an analysis lying behind each of them. The documents or statements referred to over the week end appear to have been taken from some of the working papers that have been under discussion with the provincial governments. As I said, those papers indicated a range of possible dates commencing next October 14 and running into the next year for the possible termination of controls. No decision on this point has been taken by the government as yet. We have not had a full and definitive response from the provincial governments as yet.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM POSSIBILITY OF PROGRAM ENDING ON OCTOBER 14 AND THAT RATE OF INFLATION REDUCED TO FOUR PER CENT BY JANUARY,
speechtext: Is the minister saying that the October 14 date is not a possible date for the termination of controls, and when will he get rid of the uncertainty which is dominating the economy? When will business and the people in this country learn from the government when these controls will be terminated or what the government's views on them are? I ask this question particularly in relation to the fact of the continuing decline in the confidence of business, which seems to be apparent in the figures for the last quarter of last year with respect to real growth.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION PROGRAM POSSIBILITY OF PROGRAM ENDING ON OCTOBER 14 AND THAT RATE OF INFLATION REDUCED TO FOUR PER CENT BY JANUARY,
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman asked whether this is a possible date. I indicated there was a range of dates set out for the provincial governments. The position we have taken in this regard is that in a program of this kind, which was brought into effect with the co-operation of the provincial governments, it is entirely reasonable for them to be fully consulted on the possible dates for the termination of the program. In that sense, we have gone to the provinces and put to them a series of solutions and sought their response. It seems clear from this that the government of Canada will have to make its choice among possible dates, but I think it makes sense to have full consultation. I hope we can have definitive responses from the provinces at a very early date, in which

case I, too, would look forward to the possibility of making a statement on the projected termination date. However, until we have had the full consultation it would be difficult to make a final determination.

A regional rate of pay structure was proposed with different rates of pay for the following regions: Maritimes, Quebec, Ontario, Yukon and Northwest Territories, Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia. In addition, however, the two parties to the agreement requested exclusion of payments made in both guideline years to react to both emphasized recruiting and retention difficulties. The parties argued the exclusion of these payments on the basis of Schedule C of the AIB Compensation regulations which deal, in part, with vacancy rates and recruiting plus retention difficulties. The AIB decision allowed the exclusion and approved the collective agreement as negotiated. In the Maritime Region the annual rate for the working level therapists is as follows: Effective December 29, 1975, $11,225 to $12,995; Effective June 28, 1976, $12,011 to $13,905; Effective December 27, 1976, $12,491 to $14,461; Effective June 27, 1977, $12,991 to $15,039.

The agreement provided for a compensation increase of 29.91 per cent. This increase related to an arithmetic guideline of 14.09 per cent for the group's first guideline year. The parties could not support a historical relationship argument and did not present detailed information for exclusions on the same basis as the Federal Government therapists. The AIB decision was to allow the arithmetic guideline increase of 14.09 per cent for the first year. The parties have implemented a further 12 per cent increase for the second year from April 1, 1976 to Marclf 31, 1977. We believe, as well, that our educational and retraining system must reflect more closely the manpower needs of the country. This relates directly to the issue before us. In this respect I would like to point out that the Senate committee report on Canada Manpower, published some five months ago, said that employers see the Manpower centres, and 1 quote-
Chiefly as a source of unskilled labour-very few regard the Manpower service as place to recruit highly skilled, managerial or professional employees.
The Department of Manpower and Immigration is expected to spend a total of about $833 million this Fiscal year. The money is there and it is being spent. However, because of confused government priorities much of it is being misused and, indeed, wasted. Even in the peak years of Manpower spending in 1972-73 only 32 per cent of the Manpower budget went into direct job creation. Most of the rest went, and even today goes, into training and into Manpower centres even though the Canada Manpower centres are known to have an extremely poor placement record and the training all too often equips people for jobs that do not even exist on the labour market. The government has more than adequate staff, I believe, and more than adequate resource personnel to forecast what will happen in the economy and to take corrective action. There are at the present time three or four quite prestigious forecasting institutions that are actually doing that job. I believe the government would do well to avail themselves of this material in order to lay out a program that will provide a solution and reduce the unemployment rate we face today.
Bill C-27 proposes to implement the integration of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the Department of Manpower and Immigration to become the Canada employment and immigration commission. This is something we have been looking forward to. In fact, we never agreed with the department being split up when that was done some years ago. It did not make sense to separate a department concerned with finding jobs from the agency concerned with paying unemployment benefits-unless, of course, the Unemployment Insurance Commission were to become mainly an agency for the redistribution of income. I suspect this is the reason the government made the change some years ago.
We have felt for some time that too easy entrance into the program has had an unfortunate effect on the work ethic in Canada. We have felt, and have been advocating, that the qualifying period for unemployment insurance beneFits should be increased from eight weeks to 12 weeks, recognizing, however, the regional inequalities of job opportunities. We are advocating, as well, that the governor in council maintain the right to make special provisions in areas of extremely high and chronic unemployment such as, for instance, Newfoundland and the maritimes. My colleague, the hon. member for Hamil-
Employment and Immigration
ton West (Mr. Alexander), gave notice of the amendment he intends to move on behalf of our party covering this situation.
An overhaul and simplification of the benefit structure is good news as well. Presently the regulations are, to my mind, unnecessarily complicated, as evidence by the number of people who contact their member of parliament about unemployment insurance claims. Many are completely baffled by the system, and even after their claim has been processed they are not sure why they are receiving benefits other than knowing that they paid into the plan for so many years. If that is the way it is looked upon by those receiving benefits, how much more difficult is it to explain to those who do not qualify for benefits why they are in that situation?
We all know that just because a person pays into the unemployment insurance scheme for ten or 20 years that does not ensure he can claim benefits for that length of time. The plain fact is that many people look upon unemployment insurance as a pension or retirement plan of some sort. I hope the new benefit structure and new procedures will emphasize the fact that this is an insurance plan and not welfare, pension or some other form of redistribution of income. On a number of occasions I have raised the point, as have others, that in many instances it seems to be too easy to receive benefits under the unemployment insurance program. But the other day I came across an article in a newspaper that pointed out that department was going to continue searching the records to make sure those who are receiving benefits under the plan are justified in doing so. I believe that is as it should be.
A great many people are bothered, however, that some people receive unemployment insurance benefits for a long period of time after perhaps working only a short while, yet others who have been working for many years and paying into the scheme are cut off after receiving three or four months of benefits. That situation should be looked into, Mr. Speaker. I can give one instance right on point. I received a communication from a lady who had worked in the same place for about 13 years, paying unemployment insurance premiums. The shopping centre where she was working was destroyed by fire. She was given about three weeks to find alternate employment. This lady was possibly over 50 years of age. Although she had been working for many years, she did not own a car and walked to work. She had to try to find alternate employment at least until the shopping centre was rebuilt. After three weeks she was told that was long enough to find alternate employment and she was cut off benefits even though she had tried in other areas as well to find work. In fact, she went to a major community about 30 miles away and made inquiries. Everywhere she went she was told there was a list of people ahead of her and there did not seem to be any possibility of work.
It seems as though these people are forced to journey back and forth considerable distances to try to find employment in other communities, yet the stores in those communities have lists of local people also seeking employment. If they were to hire the one from out of town it would leave someone in their own community unemployed. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker,

Yes, still practising. To repeat, when I go home on weekends and sit in my office between nine o'clock and three p.m., I find that half the people coming to me have unemployment insurance problems. One must endure the emotional spectacle of watching a man in his fifties crying because his unemployment insurance has run out and he must fall back on welfare. People like that, through no fault of their own, are unemployed. They do not control the economy; they do not have the economic input of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), other cabinet ministers, or our captains of industry. Some of these people remain unemployed for several months, sometimes for as long as one or two years. Such unemployment leads to tremendous family conflict and personal depression-depression which needs medical treatment.
The government's proposals as embodied in this bill puzzle me. Why, when more people are out of work in this country than at any time since the great depression, does the government want to tighten up unemployment insurance? Why is it changing the qualifying period? There is no logic to it. As far as I am concerned, it is immoral. Neither the government nor industry can move the economy forward. Approximately one million people are out of work, and the government chooses this very time to tighten unemployment insurance. Why? I suggest that the government is bending to the wish of a minority of rednecks, is bending the wishes of people who don't know the first thing about unemployment. They have picked out one or two examples in their communities to show that somebody has been caught ripping off the UIC fund. They

therefore think that a great minority of recipients, or even the majority, are cheating on UIC. Once and for all, let us put that myth to rest.
On February 1, 1977, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) tried to convey desperately to this House and the country that Canada has the most advanced employment and job insurance programs in the world. Although official figures show 889,000 people as being unemployed, the minister was able to say with a straight face and serious-minded mien that Manpower services generally, as well as the newer job-creation programs, have been greatly strengthened and matured in the past ten years. After hearing this, someone was led to comment that if we have much more of this kind of strength and maturity we shall most likely be doomed.
I want to concentrate on two main aspects of the bill, the integration of the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the Unemployment Insurance Commission, and the charges in entrance requirements which must be met if one is to obtain benefits under the unemployment insurance scheme. I touched on the latter point briefly in my opening remarks. I wish to review these changes within the context of our present economic situation and then assess the effect of the proposals on those presently unemployed and on others who will no doubt be uprooted from their jobs in the months to come.
As various spokesmen have said, our number one economic problem in Canada is unemployment. My party has been stressing this point for the past two years. Finally, in the past few months the government has begun to recognize that employment is our number one problem. Official figures published by Statistics Canada show that more than 889,000 men and women in this country are now unemployed. I stress "official" figures because, as my leader showed, those figures do not take into account the hidden unemployed, those who have simply given up looking for non-existent jobs. They are the hidden unemployed. I submit that there are at least 450,000 people among the hidden unemployed, and if you add their numbers to the official figure the real unemployment rate rises to approximately 11 per cent. That is a disgustingly large figure for this country.
In my riding, Brant, Canada Manpower officials recently listed 4,261 people as unemployed. That was the last figure available, in January. At the same time there were 106 job vacancies listed in my constituency which has a population of over 100,000. In all the country there are only 42,000 job vacancies at present. This means that if every job vacancy were filled, 889,000 people would still remain out of work. If you add to that number the number of the hidden unemployed, you can see that more than one million people altogether would be out of work in this country. At present more than one million individuals in this country have no recourse except apply for unemployment insurance. Their livelihood depends on it. Canadians have every right to ask why, in this rich country, this is allowed to happen. The answer is straightforward: the government does not care any more. If it did, the Minister of Finance would not wait until April before introducing a new budget.
February 28, 1977

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
The magnitude of our unemployment, aside from the misery it is inflicting on our people, is costing Canadians millions of dollars in lost productivity and extra money spent on social assistance programs. The social services office in the city of Brantford, Ontario, is currently handling between 25 and 30 requests for assistance a day. I am often accused of coming from the "golden horse shoe" area where everybody is a millionaire or worth at least half a million dollars. I am cataloguing the situation in Brantford because it is one of the relatively wealthy parts of Canada. I am informed that the number of out-of-province requests is increasing as well. The administrator of the social services office in my constituency stated that last year $33,000 was' spent assisting people who had moved to Brant county from other provinces looking for work. Those people had come from provinces where unemployment exceeded 15 per cent. They do not want hand-outs. They move into the area in the hope of finding employment. They do not want make-work programs which last for three months or even six months. They want jobs on which they can depend. Unfortunately, the job situation is disastrous not only in my constituency, but right across the country.
Further, forecasts for the months to come are gloomy. The consensus among economists is that the unemployment situation will worsen before it gets better. Referring again to my own constituency, local businessmen do not expect any improvement in the unemployment situation for the coming year, this at a time when it is being rumoured that there might be an election within the next few months. This is rather interesting.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
We are, but you sure as heck aren't. It is against this background that we should examine this bill. The minister, in his preamble during debate on this bill, would have us believe that everything is coming up roses. Like his predecessor, he is very conversant with the services his department renders. The minister and his colleagues take great pride in the unemployment insurance scheme we have in this country. Like his predecessor, the minister is of the opinion that unemployment is not really a serious problem because our unemployment insurance scheme relieves the unemployed of the worst financial hardships that used to go with the loss of a job.
Possibly that is the reason this government has totally neglected the underlying problem that job opportunities were not, and are not, developing fast enough to keep pace with the growth of the labour force. The minister is shaking his head. Why, then, do we have nearly a million peqple out of work? Answer that. Instead of spending its time developing policies which would create more jobs and get people off unemployment insurance, this government is preoccupied with possible abuses of the insurance scheme. Dealing with those very few people who abuse the unemployment insurance system during
Employment and Immigration
this period of high unemployment shows that the government has a somewhat warped sense of priorities. This is an affront to all those who are legitimately receiving payments as a result of something totally beyond their control.
As W. A. Wilson stated in an article in the Montreal Star:
For all the fears that the insurance system has been exploited, human beings are by nature active, and for most men and women, this means that they work and indeed want to work.
Mr. Wilson added something else which I want to stress especially to some members to my right. He said:
The maximum benefits from UIC are generous enough in terms of keeping the wolf from the door, but they must seem small to a wage earner who becomes unemployed and finds the payments on his automobile or television set do not fit in to his reduced income.
This reduced income comes about overnight. We talk about an average pay-out of $94 a week. What about the emotional effect on the breadwinner, the head of the family, going from $200 a week down to $94 a week? We still hear people say that that person would rather get $94 a week and do nothing than the $200 he was getting while gainfully employed. That is a psychological jam which some people in this country- indeed, a few in this House-have that I do not understand. According to recent statistics, and I am repeating myself here, the average pay-out is $94.56. That was as of November, 1976-just a few months ago.
This leads me to discuss the main purpose of Bill C-27, which is to change the entrance requirements for unemployment insurance benefits. The minister said in the House that the main reasons for changing the entrance requirements were that the present system provides too many people with a disincentive to work, that eight to 11-weekers are mainly individuals without dependants, young, or secondary earners and for that reason, following the minister's logic, they really do not require financial assitance. Furthermore, the current entrance requirements reinforce unstable work patterns. I believe that is a quote from the minister's speech. I want to deal with each of these arguments in turn.
The view that the present unemployment system is a disincentive to work is not novel. The only problem with this view is that it is not supported by facts. Even the eight weeks of steady work needed to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits can be hard to come by when job seekers outnumber jobs by almost 20 to one. The minister does not understand or, even worse, does not know that in many parts of this country it is extremely difficult, if not impossible, to get even eight weeks of work. At least the former minister, despite his shortcomings, with respect to this aspect of unemployment insurance acknowledged that increasing the qualifying period was not the way to tighten up the unemployment insurance system. In May, 1975-and that is not a generation ago-the former minister had this to say about the qualifying period, and I quote from his statement in the House:
-if you examine where those short term attachment people are, you will find that they coincide with areas of this country that have the more chronic conditions of high unemployment-

February 28, 1977
Employment and Immigration
He went on to say, as was pointed out by those members of my party who were on a fact-finding trip to Atlantic Canada:
-they occur in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces to a higher degree because the conditions of disparity there are such that people get marginal jobs which are almost coincidental with short term attachment jobs-
The minister mentioned the young as those who would probably lose out as a result of this change. I suppose he is suggesting young people in this country have no incentive to work. If he cared to examine the present situation, he would realize that the young do want to work. Many university graduates are accepting menial jobs and are accepting positions which underemploy them. But the basic fact remains: There are about 387,000 unemployed between the ages of 15 and 24 and they, along with the over-25 group are currently scrambling for the some 41,000 jobs that are available in Canada. Instead of creating satisfying, fulfilling jobs for these people, the minister simply eliminates many from unemployment insurance rolls. That is what will happen if this bill passes.
The other group affected by this change is secondary earners, many of whom are housewives. We are led to believe that these individuals do not really need financial assistance; they do not need to work. This is sheer nonsense, and the minister knows it. The Minister of Finance, during debate on the income tax bill, stated that the average income in Canada in 1975 was $16,232. That average income was derived in most cases as a result of two or more people working in the family. It has become an economic necessity over the past ten years for both spouses to earn an income in order to make ends meet. Finally, it was suggested that the current entrance requirements reinforce unstable work patterns.
I would ask, Mr. Speaker, what are the effects of prolonged joblessness? Does this government even consider the frustration, the deteriorating morale caused by lengthy idleness? What, for that matter, are the effects of temporary jobs? I refer here to the type of jobs created by the minister's employment strategy. Make-work programs may have short-term social benefits, but as the Economic Council of Canada pointed out last year they can also have a debilitating long-run effect. Make-work programs such as LIP and Canada Works, Young Canada Works, and so on, do not and were never intended to provide permanent employment. As many of us know, having been involved with the LIP program, the main dissatisfaction among LIP workers is the lack of job security. This is the very thing we should be trying to eliminate in this country. We should be providing job security, not insecurity.
We know, from studies carried out, that programs such as LIP do not contribute a significant stepping-stone to regular employment for unemployed, marginal or poor workers. Rather, for a substantial majority of participants in make-work projects the job constitutes a temporary source of employment income, to be followed by unemployment, labour force withdrawal, another make-work project, social assistance or a combination thereof. They get themselves into a vicious circle. They go on a LIP project. They are there for six months. The project terminates and they are thrown back on
(Mr. Blackburn.]
the labour market. They go through the process of seeking employment. They draw unemployment insurance benefits. They carry out an active job search. Before they know it, they are called upon by some person who was lucky enough to get a grant for a LIP program. "How would you like to come back?" The man answers, "Well, 1 have just got on unemployment insurance, so why should I get off unemployment insurance and go back to LIP?" He is talked into it, and he goes back to LIP. He works another three or four months and the same thing happens again under that program.
tf)
Hon. members opposite know what happens in practice as opposed to what happens in law. These people get into a cycle and they find themselves asking, at the age of 20, 40 or 50, "I do not have a permanent livelihood ahead of me; I am going from one job-creation program to another; there is no permanent aspect about what 1 am doing." I wonder how many of us around this place would feel if we knew we had no future at all. I am not talking about being defeated, but suppose we knew there was nothing there of substance for us should we be defeated in politics, or should we decide to resign, except the unemployment insurance fund, even though we are not entitled to it? I wonder how such a situation would affect us. I am not saying we are a special group in this country. We are citizens in the same way as everyone else. But would it affect the way we legislate? At times we tend to forget there are a lot of people outside the House who depend upon us for a reasonably happy and secure future. I fear that these make-work projects are becoming a permanent fixture under this government. No longer is permanent employment a goal. I strongly urge the minister to determine what kind of work patterns are being reinforced by this binge of make-work projects.
To conclude my remarks on the proposed changes in the entrance requirements I should, again, like to quote the former minister of manpower and immigration. Speaking on the qualifying period, he said:
I think it is a bit of a red herring. I think there are other areas in the act which have to be tidied up, areas which are far more significant than the favourite whipping boy of the short work claimant.
That is what the former minister said about a year ago. Now everything has changed drastically. These are my sentiments. I do not support these changes which would penalize individuals for something which is entirely out of their control. If a person does not want to work, don't give him anything. That is his choice, as I said at the beginning of my remarks. The vast majority of those who are unemployed today are people who have no control over the economy or over the business decisions of the various factories or institutions in which they work. They have no control over politics, either, except when there is an election.
At the same time, I cannot support the amendment introduced by the Conservatives which would allow for selective reduction in the qualifying period from 12 to eight weeks. It is obvious that the party to my right introduced this amendment not on the basis of known fact but, rather, on the basis of the number of votes to be gained. They do not care about the
February 28, 1977

welfare of the citizens of this country. This was shown by the way they voted on the tax bill on February 14, only a few days ago. It has also been shown in the course of the debate on the bill we are presently considering. On February 2, the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) commended the government for bringing in the 12-week qualifying period. As far as he is concerned, unemployment insurance is a means of getting something for nothing. His colleague from St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) said on the same day that this was not the time to tamper with the provisions of the act in such a way as to increase the qualifying period from eight to 12 weeks. In typical Conservative fashion, members to my right have straddled the fence and opted for selective reductions in the qualifying period.
Obviously, this was a device for gaining support in those areas of the maritimes where unemployment is so high and where it is difficult to get a job for five or six weeks, let alone for eight or 12 weeks. That is the kind of politicking I do not like. We are all Canadians, and we should all be treated equally and do everything possible to hold the country together in a positive way. When you start making changes to suit various areas of the country, you are just putting another nail into the coffin of the country and dividing it more than it is now.
When I came here in 1971, this country was not too badly divided. When the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was elected in 1968 there was not one Parti Quebecois member elected to the legislative assembly in Quebec. Look at the situation today. After nine or ten years during which the present government has been in office we have a bitterly divided country. It is not just Quebec. We have western alienation-Alberta, British Columbia and the prairies. Yes, and Ontario too; northern Ontario. I am not blaming the Prime Minister entirely for this, but I hope he does not go on one more of those emotional binges he went on in 1968 and try to tell the people of Canada that he is the only federal leader who can keep the country together, when the country today is more divided than when he was elected nine years ago.

speechtext:
1 appreciate your advice, Mr. Speaker, and will do so. If the Conservative amendment were to be passed we would have a situation whereby an individual unemployed in Steinbach, Manitoba, would not be entitled to benefits, whereas someone in St. John's East would be. I have come to accept this kind of thinking from the government benches, but it now appears as though the Conservatives are competing with the government to see who can waffle the most on any issue.
I should now like to turn to the subject of integration. In a period of our economic history where close to 8 per cent or more of our population is out of work, it is ironic that the minister is now going to establish a new department of employment and immigration. I have to agree that that is the power of positive thinking, but I think it is a lot of nonsense. The minister took it as a sign of great efficiency that, as a result of the co-operation between Canada Manpower Centres and the UIC, half the claimants for unemployment insurance benefits now register with Canada Manpower Centres and such claimants constitute 70 per cent of the total clientele of the manpower service.
According to the minister, in order to improve these superior services-I underline "superior" services-integration is a must. I suggest that, before the minister proceeds with this move, he takes a look at the shortcomings of the present system, and indeed there are many of them. I think we would have to admit that Canada Manpower Centres and the Unemployment Insurance Commission have not really worked in harmony. In many instances they have worked against each other. I know for a fact, having talked to one or two employees of Canada Manpower, they sure as heck do not want to be loaded with unemployment insurance problems.
Manpower services at the present time are woefully inadequate. That is the consensus in any given neighbourhood or community. This has been pointed out both by the Senate committee that investigated this matter and also by the Economic Council of Canada in its report entitled "People and Jobs".
Both these reports said that employers see Manpower Centres chiefly as a source of unskilled labour. Canada Manpower Centres are used for only 25 to 35 per cent of the total number of hirings that occpr during the year. Many of those, I might add, are in the category of which I spoke earlier, namely, of very temporary nature. Furthermore, a considerable number of the jobs listed by many Manpower Centres are in the primary sectors where turnover is high and employers simply put in standing orders.
Another legitimate complaint about Manpower services was brought to my attention by the United Steel Workers of America. We have witnessed, over the years, situations where companies which are in dispute with their employees list vacancies with local manpower offices. This happened again

February 28, 1977
Employment and Immigration
recently in Scarborough, where workers at Wyandotte Chemicals have been on legal strike seeking a first contract since November. During the strike area manpower offices have posted employment openings for the company. Although these notices indicate that a labour dispute is in progress, nevertheless they encourage people to interfere in a legal dispute between a company and its employees. As a staff representative of the United Steelworkers of America said in a recent letter, Manpower seems prepared to help companies make a profit even when they face a legal strike; why do they not provide the same kind of help to workers when they are locked out? That is a good question. Someone should ask the Minister of Manpower in the question period how he would answer that. There is no provision in this bill to deal with this situation. The government is quite content to continue this policy of what I call legal scabbing.
Generally speaking then, Mr. Speaker, most of the jobs registered at Canada Manpower Centres are unattractive, frequently of relatively temporary nature, low paying, and non-unionized or not organized in any way. As the Economic Council of Canada was forced to conclude, these factors limit the over-all effectiveness of Canada Manpower Centres and adversely affect their public image.
I am not addressing my criticisms directly to the counsellors who work in Canada Manpower Centres; 1 am simply saying that the way the centres are structured they are not doing their job efficiently. They are not doing the job for which they were originally set up. This is not really the fault of the employees. It is the fault of our economic system; it is the fault of employers in many cases who look upon Manpower Centres as a source of cheap labour, not expert, skilled or even semi-skilled.
The minister is quite content, ignoring these facts, to proceed to rationalize and to harmonize the present services to provide a one stop service to clients. It matters not that the present services are virtually useless. The minister hopes that integration will eliminate whatever defects exist. Most important, how does the minister hope to overcome the problem of matching-and this is a very conservative figure-the 750,000 job searchers with the 41,000 available jobs? No flow charts or diagrams will accomplish this, regardless of what the minister says.
This bill also promises financing for on the job retraining, administration of labour market programs and the policies underlying these programs. Pumping more money into training programs and into make-work programs will not alleviate unemployment. The only way to deal with unemployment is to create a job for each and every Canadian who wants one.
I conclude on this note, Mr. Speaker. I do not care if Manpower and UIC reach 100 per cent efficiency. I do not care if LIP, Canada Works and Young Canada Works achieve 100 per cent efficiency within their terms of reference. I do not care how efficient any government department is in the country today. Unless we can get the economy moving and provide jobs for the 750,000 or 800,000 people-we might even say the one million people-who are looking for work, then it does not

matter how much money we spend on make work programs, temporary jobs and all the rest; there will still be ill-feeling and restlessness in the country which will increase over the years. If we cannot solve reasonably well the economic problems of the country and create more jobs, then what is the point of spending all this money and energy on make work projects? What is the point of even taking a serious look at Bill C-27 when it is not going to alleviate the basic problem of providing meaningful work for people who want it?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while Bill C-27 deals with various matters, I wish to make only a few comments on certain amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. As I understand it, there are three major changes to be made to the act. In his speech on second reading the minister listed, first of all, the increase in the number of weeks a person must work before being entitled to draw benefits which, as the House knows, is from eight weeks to 12; the second change is in the benefits structure, which is the framework used to determine the duration of a claimant's entitlement; the third change is the outlining of more productive and developmental uses of unemployment insurance funds, such as income maintenance for persons taking approved training courses, job creation projects, and work-sharing programs. It is not my intention to comment on all of the changes, even though I realize their importance. Some contain pitfalls, some are improvements.
Job training is a subject on which I could spend 40 or 50 minutes. The minister and I have discussed it both in the House and outside the House, and it is difficult to know what the minister of labour in the province of Nova Scotia is looking for so far as training is concerned. He has made some loud statements about all the training that is going to take place, but in the meantime at the Point Edward training school in Cape Breton instructors are being laid off. However, I will deal with that on another occasion.
I should like to discuss first the increase from eight to 12 weeks of employment before entitlement to unemployment insurance benefits is achieved by those who are no longer employed. I believe, as other speakers have said, that this amendment is a backward step. It discriminates against that area of the country where the rate of unemployment is very high. As is the case in most regions of Quebec, the Atlantic provinces and the constituency which I represent suffer from a very high rate of unemployment.
I am glad to see here the hon. member for Bonaventure-Jles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Bechard) who last Friday told the whole story. His words are worth quoting. He made a very commendable speech, as he always does. Those comments which I wish to quote are to be found on page 3446 of Hansard. I trust the minister will listen very carefully to this. The hon. member said:
It remains-I am willing to admit this-that even with the best scheme, a number of unemployed could not find a job. In cases such as those which are found in the Magdalen Islands and elsewhere in my constituency, as well as in
February 28, 1977

the Gaspe Peninsula generally, including the Gaspe and Matane constituencies, and some neighbouring areas, the whole Restigouche area, the Gloucester area and New Brunswick as a whole, it should be possible, wherever the industrial base,is very limited, to adopt special measures, as mentioned by previous speakers, until such a time at least when the government decides to organize the economy in a way which would guarantee a more permanent employment of our active population.
I certainly commend the hon. gentleman for that statement because it spells out the problems with which we are confronted in the Atlantic region and in most areas of the province of Quebec. He went on to say:
Just as the duration of benefits varies and the number of weeks increases depending on the difference between the local or regional rate of unemployment and the national average, so, in my humble opinion should the number of working weeks before obtaining benefits vary in the case of the Magdalen Islands and the Gaspe peninsula in general, as well as the New Brunswick and the Atlantic provinces ridings. Let us put an end to the ridiculous practice whereby an applicant must file evidence that he is looking for a job in a region such as ours where there are few openings, if any. Instead we should require all employers to report job openings to Canada Manpower offices, including those they fill themselves without going to the Manpower Centres. This way Manpower officials will always know what jobs are available.
This is good advice from the hon. member for Bonaventure-iles-de-la-Madeleine. As he said, we are faced with a situation where people get tired going to Manpower offices and hearing the same story over and over again that no work is available. They are told they must make a job search. They go to see five or six employers who tell them that there is nothing available. This is ridiculous. We know there is no employment in the first place. The Manpower officials know that. It is no reflection on them. They do the best they can to place people.
For example, in the Sydney office the latest report for January, 1977, showed that the number of those seeking employment was 13,134 and there were only 210 job vacancies, so you can see what they are faced with. As was mentioned by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) on Friday, this is the situation. In his riding the official unemployment figure was 29,000, but when he investigated it thoroughly at the Manpower offices he discovered that the actual figure was 60,000.
I do not understand why the government is bringing in this bill now. I recall very vividly that when it was first introduced it was supposed to be the greatest thing since Bryce Mackasey, not since sliced bread. Here we are with our unemployment rate higher than it has ever been. We are making it more difficult for people who are truly serious and honest in trying to find work to receive a few dollars. I am not trying to protect those who abuse the fund. I condemn the judges and the magistrates who tap them over the fingers, people who are guilty of defrauding the system and of defrauding the government. All they are told is, "Don't you boys do any more of this, and everything will be all right". We should condemn them and give them the severest of penalties. Remember the postal strike when we discovered the ski bums who were not there to collect their cheques? There were none from the Atlantic provinces or the eastern regions of Quebec among them, because in most of those areas people cannot afford to buy ski equipment, let alone go skiing and collect unemployment insurance.
Employment and Immigration
It is great for members of boards of directors sitting in back rooms to say that, "So and so does not want to work anyhow, so cut him off." That is absolutely incorrect. I think the frequency of abuses is minimal, particularly in the regions about which we are talking.
As 1 said, in my constituency in industrial Cape Breton where the rate of unemployment is very high it is very difficult to obtain an accurate figure. It is estimated to be somewhere between 25 per cent and 30 per cent. I hope it is less than that, but I am afraid the rate is even higher. I know the sources of employment in that area and 1 know they are shrinking, while the labour force is growing. It is difficult to justify the change, and 1 can tell you that those arguments have no validity whatsoever in the region that I represent.
The minister and others have tried to justify this amendment by stating that it is an incentive, especially for young people, to work longer. All I can say is that this argument does not apply to either the younger or the older workers in my area, in the Atlantic region or in eastern Quebec. The young people there do not need incentives to stay in the work force. Their big problem is more to get into the labour force and obtain employment in the first place, than to keep it. Those who may be in and out of the active work force are the victims of an economically depressed area. I can tell you this, Mr. Speaker, because I know these young people.
As many other hon. members do, I discussed this with the young people and also with my older constituents. 1 know they are anxious to be part of the active work force, and it is a sad state of affairs when they do get a job that it only lasts for a few weeks. Certainly they would rather work than be on unemployment insurance. They would love to have a permanent job. They would love to have job security so they could plan their future with confidence, free from the worry and anxiety of loss of work.
To say there is a 25 per cent or 30 per cent rate of unemployment is startling. Of course other people talk about a rate of 14 per cent or 15 per cent, but 25 per cent to 30 per cent is terrible.
These statistics are called hard figures. Personally, I think of those men and women who make up these percentages, and when I hear the word "claimant" or "bodies"-bureaucratic lingo-in reference to the unemployed, I think it is shocking. I think of the man or woman seeking employment or seeking unemployment insurance as human beings. In so far as industrial Cape Breton is concerned, I deny most vigorously that the number of people in and out of employment has increased and that these people are doing so of their own free will. They are doing so from necessity, not from choice. I agree that if there are abuses under the U1C Act then those abuses should be corrected, but not by increasing the period of employment from eight to 12 weeks. An abuse will not be corrected and a real hardship will be inflicted.
I noticed that in his speech on second reading the minister also mentioned that unemployment insurance will continue to provide a measure of income protection to unemployed workers while they conduct an active search for jobs to locate the

February 28, 1977
Employment and Immigration
most suitable and satisfying employment available to them. This puts the pressure on the individuals, and that is only right because he or she should go and look for jobs. But surely if a Canada Manpower Centre, which is the official government employment agency of the federal government, does not know where there are jobs, where will the people find jobs? They will have to go through this phony deal of going to a series of businessmen and being told there are no jobs available. They know that from the beginning.
I only wish there were no necessity for this active search for jobs in my area. The time is past when they have to conduct this solitary, ineffectual search for work. If employment is not available-and the officers should know whether or not it is available-then the insurance should continue to be paid under the legislation. For whom will this create a hardship? It will create a hardship for fishermen, lumbermen, fish plant workers, construction workers, and all those who work part time. I commend the minister for changing what is commonly known as the four-week rule. It is proposed that it be done away with. At the present time it results in a claim being terminated if benefits are not paid for four consecutive weeks in an extended benefit period.
This rule is considered a serious disincentive to individuals who might otherwise take short-term jobs. There are many hundreds of people caught in that trap. There people are anxious and willing to work, particularly construction workers, fish plant workers and so forth. They go back for a day, two days, or three days, and they think they re-qualify. However, they are told that they are out, that they do not have any chance to collect benefits or to continue collecting benefits. This will continue, as others have said, to put more people on welfare, but the municipalities cannot stand it. At the moment it is difficult for municipalities in the regions I have mentioned to get by. They just cannot afford to pay more welfare, and people will just be hungry.
I am not being dramatic or anything else when I say that there are people on Cape Breton Island who are losing their homes. They cannot pay the cost of electric heating. They cannot pay their mortgages. They formerly worked at the steel plant. Their benefits are running out quickly, and some have already run out. There is no way for them to carry on. If we adopt this measure, we will make it much more serious than it ever was before. It will take millions of dollars out of the economy in those areas of the country where it is needed most.
Some ask-the previous speaker included-why we should pass a law to suit certain regions of the country? This government and previous governments have done that to suit certain regions of the country. We cannot pass a blanket law which will treat everybody equitably across this vast country. I spoke to a Liberal member from Saskatchewan the other day. I asked him what is the employment rate out there and he said it is 2.8 per cent. Well, now, that is rather nice.

speechtext:
I doubt that. At any rate, I would be less than frank with the government and this House if I did not reaffirm that I cannot under any circumstances but oppose in every way available to me the proposals contained in this package of amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I wonder if in this package there is anything to deal with a case whereby a group of whizz-kids came to a regional office and to local offices to conduct so-called investigations as to the possibility of alleged padding of placements. I do not know if that is quite correct. It is supposed to have happened. I trust the minister is listening very carefully. In the interim three senior people who have 30, 40 or 50 combined years' service in the public service were suspended immediately for a week with pay. No charges were laid. There was no money they could have stolen.
There is an investigation going on. These people still receive their salaries, but they have been warned not to talk to anyone in that office nor to be seen around that office. When that kind of thing is allowed I wonder what we are coming to. I do not at all blame the minister for that, but I hope and trust he will look into situations like that. In a small area if John Brown or Joe Blow is suspended, people immediately get suspicious and wonder what is going on. They think that where there is smoke there is fire, and that something has to be going on. The character of the people involved can be grievously injured because to this point nothing has been proved against these people or any of the staff in that office. I hope the minister will take this into consideration either in his legislation or investigations.
It has been mentioned by others that there are roughly 39,000 or 40,000 job vacancies across this country at the present time but that there are over one million who are unemployed. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) has been making great noises about that, and rightly so, but if hon. members would look up the comments I made here two or three years ago they would find that I said the same thing. I said that we do not get true statistical figures
February 28, 1977

because many people get tired of going to Canada Manpower Centre offices, they head out on their own and just keep chasing around anywhere they can trying to find a job on their own, therefore they are not considered as being unemployed as far as the C.M.C. is concerned. Hon. members know that. These people come to their member's offices every day and, if they do not, some hon. members must live in a wonderful part of the country. I know that places like that exist because people have come to me telling me that in Toronto there is difficulty getting employees. My goodness, I wish we had that problem on the east coast.
Coming from an area which suffers unemployment to the extent that one would have to conclude that Cape Breton in many ways is akin to the developing countries of the world, without the interest-free loans which are available to the developing countries, I probably have one of the most honest methods of describing the terrible plight of our area. If we want an example of why this nation is in a state of almost complete chaos, we need only examine the multitude of proposals which have been made in an effort to combat the problems of the Atlantic region and then to witness nothing more than lip service-and that can be lip service or LIP service-as the end result. Every question I pose and every suggestion I make in this House is taken by the various ministers of the government as if they are deeply and truly concerned about our problems, but as soon as they disappear from the House the gravity of the situation seems to disappear with them. The only result is a continuation and worsening of the problem.
In my own area I look back on the loss of General Instruments Corporation. That corporation assembled radio tuners. 1 look back on the loss of Canadian Motor Industries which assembled Toyota automobiles. I look back on the loss of Kaiser Strontium. Two years ago, as I said earlier in the House today, 3,900 employees worked at the Sydney steel plant, but that number is now down to 2,250, and there is no assurance that that figure will be maintained. I look at the drastic cut-backs by Canadian National in the Atlantic region and at the Canadian National marine services on the docks at North Sydney where in peak periods in the summer there once were 1,000 people employed. In the winter the number was about 500, 600 or 700. Now we have only about 200 working there every day. There were 1,000 people working at General Instruments, this in an area of chronic unemployment. Such industries with that kind of employment opportunity were allowed to leave. This happened under the Trudeau and Regan administrations. What would have been required to keep General Instruments or Canadian Motor Industries in operation there would probably have been far less than the amount which has already been expended on unemployment benefits and welfare.
All this is not to mention the human degradation associated with any form of assistance as compared with gainful employment. No one knows better than I and other hon. members from the Atlantic region about the operation of UIC and Manpower offices, particularly in my area. Probably three
Employment and Immigration
quarters of our work is associated with the problems of constituents in securing employment or securing unemployment insurance benefits. The time which is not involved with those two operations is associated with welfare, with schemes of the Department of National Health and Welfare, the provincial department of social services and those of the Department of Veterans Affairs. People in Cape Breton need hope, and hope comes in the form of jobs. It is not a matter of taking people off the unemployment insurance rolls because they will not take the jobs available; there just are no jobs.
My efforts are geared to trying to get people enough work to get them on the unemployment rolls, and it is difficult to get that much work. It means two months work out of 12 months if this bill goes through. A number of people in Cape Breton would not qualify if this were in effect now because they have not been able to get very much work in the last 12 months. They do not even figure in the statistics. When I ask them if they have gone to the Manpower Centre they tell me they have, but there is nothing for them. They are the forgotten Canadians. Because they are not included in the unemployment statistics they do not get a passing thought from the government. Do not talk to Cape Bretoners about the break-up of Canada because the government shows more concern for the underprivileged in other parts of the world than it does for the human misery that has become their way of life.
Some will say that is a terrible thing to say when some people in the world are starving. 1 do not think there is anything wrong with foreign aid, but I do think we should try to help people in this country who are truly having problems. A week ago the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) said that he did not think anyone in this country was starving. I can tell him people are starving in this country, Mr. Speaker.
Now we are being told that the qualifying period for benefits should be increased from two months to three months- this at a time when over a million Canadians are without work. We are telling people we will legislate them off the unemployment insurance rolls and onto the welfare rolls. Mr. Speaker, I will not condone that nor will I co-operate in order to have this type of ordeal perpetrated on the people of Cape Breton Island, of the Atlantic region or of anywhere else in Canada that is having unemployment problems. This government can tell me it wants a longer qualification period for unemployment insurance benefits when it can also tell me there are jobs so that people can obtain employment long enough to qualify for benefits, or indeed work permanently so that they do not have to apply for benefits. When that happens I will be pleased to support this proposal, but not until then. I see no sign of that happening, so I was pleased that the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) moved an amendment that would maintain the present program in areas of higher unemployment than the national average. I will support that amendment, but there is no way I can support any lengthening of the present qualifying period.

February 28, 1977
Employment and Immigration
This government said a few years ago that this bill was a great thing, but there were not so many unemployed then. There are thousands more people unemployed now. If the government can live with itself after proposing such callous and unfeeling legislation let it, but I will have no part of the decision.
The terrible financial mess the government has put the country in will not be loaded on the shoulders of the working men and women of Cape Breton Island so long as I represent that area. For too long the working people of this nation have been the scapegoats of the horrendous ineptitude of the government. There has been one example after another of alleged scandal, corruption and mismanagement. The poor people are singled out as the culprits in government waste and extravagance. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and others tell the people to stop spending, but they do not have money to spend. Government spokesmen blame them for their spending and extravagance as the cause of inflation. They are much like the Romans who found themselves in the arenas facing the lions because they were the entertainment of the nobility and the mobs alike. This government tries to trample on the rights of the poor and the defenceless but, Mr. Speaker, it will do it against the strongest opposition I can muster.
It is easy to say that people will not work, but in areas of New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, and almost all of Quebec, most people try very hard to find work. They just cannot find it, Mr. Speaker.
We cannot afford the luxury of this government and its unrealistic and uncaring schemes. If we are to have a country in the future we had better meet the challenge of the people of this nation to be able to reside and work where they want to themselves. Government spokesman may say that people in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island who cannot find work should move and they will be paid a mobility grant.

speechtext: Move where?

speechtext:
Indeed, where? If they could move what are they faced with? They have worked hard all their lives to get their homes. Maybe they have a couple of children in school-even university if that is possible. If they move to Ontario or the west it is going to cost them so much to buy a home that they just cannot do it. The work has to be provided where they live and that is why I have been pressing continuously the government to do something about steel in Cape Breton which is the backbone of the economy of Nova Scotia. I think possibly the government might be trying to do something.
People in this country should be able to reside and work where they wish. That is not possible and will not be possible so long as proposals are brought forward that are so out of touch with reality. I am surprised that the minister would go along with this. I have the highest regard for him. I know that he has been out of work in his time and has had to pound the roads looking for work. He has worked in the mines as I have as a miner, and knows what that is all about. Surely he will listen to his backbenchers and not only to his bureaucratic

advisers, and think seriously about the amendment our party proposed.
I mentioned the steel situation, Mr. Speaker. Many people have been laid off. On November 25 last I posed a question to the Prime Minister regarding the possibility of the government purchasing steel rails for stockpiling. It has been done with coal, uranium, and wheat, so it could be done with steel and it would get people back to work until there is an improvement in the market. The Prime Minister gave the following reply as reported at page 1360 of Hansard'.
The hon. member raises a question which the Minister of Transport has been discussing with me and some other colleagues. It is a suggestion that has considerable merit, but as the hon. member would recognize, it requires considerable expenditures and at a time of restraint...
The Prime Minister did not completely frown upon my suggestion, so I hope he will give it consideration and people will not have to depend on unemployment insurance.
Before I resume my seat, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read from an editorial in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of February 10 written by the editor-in-chief and prominent newspaper man, Harold Shea, a former member of the Press Gallery here. Under the heading'"Unemployment Taken Calmly" he writes:
One of the most puzzling aspects of the country's current unemployment situation is that so many people are seemingly unmoved by the extend of the problem.
Those words apply to the government, but the government is unmoved. Government ministers figure that they are giving the workers many benefits; I say they are doing little to help our people find work.
I do not have time to read all of the editorial. I commend its reading to hon. members. It is available in the reading room. Perhaps I can quote one or two more sentences. The author goes on to say:
Thank Heavens there are no riots, name-calling incidents, or something worse. But neither is there much concern-even quiet concern-about the idleness, which is disgraceful and demoralizing...
Nowhere is the situation more difficult than in our own Atlantic provinces. Statistics show that in some parts of the area, unemployment is running 50 per cent above the national average.
I point out that the unemployment rate in Cape Breton Island alone is between 25 per cent and 30 per cent. I continue quoting:
The report that unemployment is rising in Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia, too, is just as worrisome, because it is these rich provinces-the Big Three-that contribute in such large measure to the equalization of wealth and services across the country.
We can't afford to yawn much longer. The government should speed up the production of the budget and get on with the job of stimulating the economy. The lethargy must end, and the sooner the better.
In conclusion, I say that no way, in no way, can I support the concept of this bill. I will not support it, despite what some hon. members, including some members of my party, say about it. They do not live in the real world or know what is happening. Some hon. members who live in or near Toronto say that they cannot find employees for their factories. Mr. February 28, 1977

Speaker, we do not even have the factories in my area. They are moving out all the time. 1 raised this question with the ministers responsible, but little has been done. I have raised those questions I mentioned earlier with industrial planners, provincial organizations, and with DREE, but little has been done.
I hope the minister will give every consideration to my remarks. If he does not wish to accept the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Hamilton West let him bring in his own amendment, or let another member of the government party propose an amendment that would give the government the credit for acting. If the unemployment rate were 4 per cent, right across the country, perhaps the government's proposal would be acceptable. But that is not the case. Therefore I plead with the minister to give every consideration to my suggestion, for the reasons I mentioned and for a heck of a lot more I did not have time to mention.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill C-27 I will attempt to keep my comments brief. All concerned are anxious to have the bill proceed to committee where the merits of the proposals are going to receive the deliberation they deserve.
The recently disclosed monthly labour force survey shows 889,000 Canadians as officially unemployed; two-fifths of these were heads of families or single people living alone. It is enough to provoke another round of hand-wringing and gnashing of teeth, but because there are commendable suggestions in the bill, which we have for years been advocating, I will try to restrict my comments to a general appraisal of the government's approach to unemployment and job creation.
Not since 1953, when the Dominion Bureau of Statistics began compiling such data, has the monthly rate of unemployment been so high. Added to these official figures are the controversial hidden unemployment statistics which range from 108,000 to 573,000. Depending on whether we consider those who looked for work in the last six months but not in the last four weeks, those who have thrown up their hands in despair, or those temporarily laid off or intending to start a new job within a month, we can conceivably get quite different interpretations of the unemployment picture.
If we continue to concentrate on figures, statistics, the attempts to define the typical unemployed Canadian, we tend to lose our perspective and turn our backs on the real issues. The situation has been labelled a human crisis. We ought to concentrate on the debilitating loss in productivity, the human degradation, the frustrations and cynicism that are fostered by having 889,000 Canadians, who are ready and willing to work, resort to transfer payments to subsist. We hear accusations that, according to the figures, secondary wage earners, wives and youths, not the principal sources of income for the family, are collecting the majority of insurance benefits. Every member has, I am sure, a thick file of correspondence from constituents complaining of lack of employment opportunities or injustices at the hands of manpower and unemployment insurance administrators.
Employment and Immigration
Some of us represent ridings that suffer proportionately greater hardships than others, either due to the lack of natural resources or the failure to accrue the full benefits of exploiting the nation's wealth. These inequities have long been recognized and programs set up to mitigate the harsher effects. Recently we saw the doubling of LIP allocations to $200 million, the addition of $50 million for labour-intensive projects in high unemployment areas and the cut in unemployment insurance premium rates for employers and workers. A $40 million program for occupational training was added, supplemented by an expansion of the Canada Manpower Mobility Program to $13.7 million.
In the final three quarters of 1976, about 39 per cent of corporation profits was paid out in corporation taxes. This helped meet the cost of a wide range of public services. Another 40 per cent was used to expand and improve productive capacity, creating and maintaining jobs for the future. But the increase in production was not sufficient to reduce unused industrial capacity appreciably. Nor, do we discover, did it reduce the unemployment rate. Although total employment rose by 2.4 per cent last year, the unemployment rate climbed marginally from 7 per cent in 1975, through 7.2 per cent in 1976, to 7.5 per cent in December of 1976. Moreover, the additional employment was not uniformly distributed among the various industrial sectors. For instance, employment declined in the export-oriented industries, reflecting the cyclical downturn of world markets. We cannot place the blame totally on world market situations, though. It is obvious that the economy as a whole should grow faster to reduce unemployment. We need a new budget, and we need it soon. Personal tax cuts, business tax concessions to promote expansion and reduced government expenditures, are requisite.
I notice that the government has abandoned its publicity campaign to convince the public that it is serious about austerity. With an increase in spending of 14 per cent, I do not blame the government. How long could you keep that type of spending spree under wraps? The effects will filter down through the economy, causing more inflation and doing nothing to create more jobs, because the spending priorities are all wrong.
Unfortunately, the expectations for the rate of recovery in the industrial world have been revised downward since the middle of 1976. We can expect Canadian exports to be adversely affected, which will reduce the external stimulus to the Canadian economy, this in turn being translated into continued high levels of unused industrial capacity and high unemployment. One is struck with the realization that conventional wisdom and traditional policies are not at all adequate to tackle the problems. In fact one wonders if the government has even selected the most popular priorities.
While a recent Gallup poll showed 48 per cent of the respondents thinking that the government should give greater attention to unemployment, only 42 per cent agreed with the Liberals that inflation was of greater concern.
There has been no dearth, either, of public sentiment on the functioning of the UIC system. It is in the context of these

February 28, 1977
Employment and Immigration
factors-Canada's labour market, the nature of our unemployment, and the history of the acceptance of the UIC scheme- that we must address the proposals included in Bill C-27.
Prior to 1966, the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the National Employment Service worked closely together, sharing the same facilities, and by close association and co-operation were readily able to discern whether or not claimants were eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. Once again the merging of these services, provided the process is properly administered and how large a bureaucracy is created, is hard to find fault with. Indeed, we have witnessed the disturbing phenomenon of job vacancies rising hand-inhand with the unemployment rate, except in some severely depressed areas. This is an indication that joblessness today has become the outgrowth of an increasingly high turnover in the labour market as more and more people abandon old jobs in search of new, more rewarding and fulfilling ones.
In British Columbia this January, for instance, there was an unemployment rate of 8.8 per cent. When broken down to sex and age we find that 6.8 per cent were men out of work, 12.2 per cent were women, and 17.6 per cent were in the 15 to 24 age bracket. The figures are slightly higher than the Canadian average but the proportions are roughly the same.
Unemployment insurance benefits have generally been touted as good for frictional unemployment, moving from job to job or re-entering the labour force after raising a family. They are also found to be beneficial for sufferers of cyclical unemployment, victims of the vagaries of the business cycles.
Although insurance benefits are not as appropriate for structural unemployment, the mismatching of skills and labour requirements, or seasonal unemployment, it could still be said that our jobless were being maintained by one of the most generous and comprehensive social security systems in the industrialized countries.
The inappropriateness and the abuses have given rise to scrutiny and study of the scheme which corroborated, to a certain degree, intuitive doubts and misgivings about the system. While induced unemployment in British Columbia, was low as compared to the ratio of induced total unemployment in Canada, residents are still inimical to tales of rip-offs. In 1976, 274 British Columbia residents were convicted of defrauding the Unemployment Insurance Commission, almost double the number in 1975.
It can be argued cogently on both sides that the change from eight weeks' work to 12 weeks' work for qualification will discourage those who flit in and out of the labour force, simply in order to qualify for benefits, or on the other hand that individuals will be deprived of the occasion to search for/ appropriate positions leading to satisfying employment. /
Our work force suffers from under-employed, over-qualified people unhappy in their unsuitable positions. In fact, the sjudy which revealed the inducement effect of insurance benefits also indicated that the greater inducement was not to quit but to remain unemployed for a longer period of time. There was
[Mr. Whittaker.)
an average of 32,000 college graduates out of work in Canada last year. How many more were under-employed? Or, what may be the level of hidden unemployment, those so discouraged with the system that they are not looking for work? We have only estimates.
Will the joining of the two services accommodate those cases where the individual legitimately takes the time to seek the employment he or she is trained for, and who won't receive compensation because he or she is classed as a new entrant to the labour force or as inexperienced, as so many housewives are labelled when they enter the labour force after raising children?
What is needed is an improved job search program, increased training funds, and job creation funds in areas of high unemployment.
Training succeeds in improving skills. It increases the productive capacity of the Canadian labour force, which in turn reduces the risk of inflationary pressures. Skill shortages are less likely to occur during periods of strong economic growth. The complaint is often heard that there is too little on-the-job training or that federally sponsored industrial training takes place primarily in small firms. These have little training capacity, or teach only skills which lead to dead-end low wage jobs.
It has to be assumed, for a program's success, that training will provide the trainee with skills to match demand and that there is some creation of skilled jobs as a spin-off from the training program. Such a program can be much more effective in stimulating employment than other fiscal measures involving the same amount of money.
Hand-in-hand with the notion of training programs goes mobility grants. It has been argued that they lack efficiency as well as equity. This does not mean mobility grants should not be given to the poor and disadvantaged; it can be learned from data that people with low incomes and with unemployment experience are more mobile than others. In fact further orientation of the Manpower Mobility Grants Program in this direction would probably have a beneficial effect in terms of income distribution.
The phenomenon of the mobile unemployed individual is probably largely misunderstood. Persons experiencing short periods of unemployment have high mobility rates. But as the duration of unemployment lengthens the mobility rate falls, and mobility rates vary inversely with the number of weeks worked. The workings of the adjustment process appear to be influenced by general economic conditions in the country as a whole. May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
February 28, 1977
