PERPETUAL BONDS, 1936 SUGGESTED REDEMPTION BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should reconsider its decision not to redeem the 3 per cent perpetual bonds, issued in 1936, through a scheme whereby (a) original purchasers would receive full face value for their bonds (b) all other holders would receive payment for each bond according to the market price for the year in which the bond was purchased (c) that an
Perpetual Bonds
immediate freeze be placed on the market value of the bonds to prevent speculation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the third time that this motion, or a variation of it, has been brought to the House for consideration at private members' time as a private members' bill. The motion should be changed slightly because the government agreed last March to redeem the bonds in 1996. The motion should now read:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should reconsider its decision not to redeem the 3 per cent perpetual bonds, issued in 1936, on September 15, 1996, and redeem them instead through a scheme whereby (a) original purchasers would receive full face value for their bonds immediately-
Parts (b) and (c) remain as printed.
The story of perpetual bonds in this House of Commons has been, I might say, perpetual. For a long time we have tried to get the government to remove these bonds from its portfolio altogether.
Perpetual bonds carry an interest rate of 3 per cent. They were bought, for the most part, in the depths of the depression by people who believed they were acquiring a security which would help them in their retirement. The government supported this idea by advertising that no one had ever lost a cent by investing in the government of Canada, so these people, who were willing to invest during the worst period of our history, economically, came forward. What happened was this: as interest rates rose during periods of inflation the value of the bonds fell. It has fallen to such a point that they are now worth around $45 or $46. In terms of real purchasing power, the people who were ready to lend the government money in the depth of the depression now hold something worth around $10. This is surely an iniquitous situation and one which ought to be remedied.
Various ministers of finance have wrestled with this problem and sought to devise means to remedy it. I believe it is recognized that it is patently unfair to those Canadians who now hold these bonds, senior citizens, most of them, that they should have no hope of getting their money back.
When the former minister of finance announced a retirement date of 1996, it did have the effect of increasing the yield on the bonds as anticipated. The difficulty is that '96 is not a realistic date because most of the people who bought the bonds back in 1936 will be dead by then. It is important that these people should be able to get their money back, money which they lent to the government in good faith. This is why it is essential that members on all sides should support my proposal.
The bonds themselves are a very small thing in the total portfolio of the government's debt but they represent a big consideration for those few thousand people who still hold them, perhaps the difference between a reasonable lifestyle and none whatsoever. It is not a matter of much consequence for the government to get rid of this $55 million in perpetual bonds. There are no others of the kind in the portfolio. They were put out only once. They are not an integral part of the

Canadian debt structure. To ask the purchasers to wait until '96 is an unconscionable thing to do because at that time many of them will not be around.
There is no question but that there has been some trading in this issue. There is no question but that there may have been some speculation. There is no question but that some people might have taken advantage of the government's action to reap some sort of windfall gain-those who bought the bonds in the last years of depressed prices from people who were forced by circumstances to sell them. But this is inconsequential when measured against the benefits which could be gained by redeeming these bonds at face value for the benefit of the people who have kept them and whose badly needed resources went into their purchase.
I think this is the third time I have spoken on this subject. There is not a single party in the House which at one time or another, through one of its members, has not addressed this question seeking an improvement in the present position. It would seem to me to be a matter of showing humanity on the part of the government in a day and age when government generally is remote from the concerns of the population. It would be an indication that governments, no matter how large, can still be concerned about the individual.
Redeeming these bonds at face value would make little difference to the government's investment picture. It would get this type of security out of the portfolio and, once and for all, we could get this issue settled to the advantage of those who bought these bonds in good faith in the thirties.

Mr. Speaker, I want to commend the mover of this motion. If anyone deserves a reward for effort, it is he. He is not the first to raise this matter. I remember that in a previous parliament Mr. Steve Otto showed an interest in this subject. He was a supporter of the government and he explored in debates during the private members' hour, as we are doing today, various measures which he thought the government should undertake.
I, too, find some difficulty in understanding exactly what the hon. member wishes to do, though I wish to make it quite clear that I am in total agreement with his assertion that something should be done. However, I think the cause would be best served if we knew exactly what the hon. member had in mind. Like the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), who attempted to put a question a few moments ago, I have some difficulty with regard to the third part of the motion. It

asks that a freeze be placed on the value of the bonds. How could this be done in a free society? The hon. member is well skilled in financial matters. He is by no means an amateur. 1 think it is clear what the government should do.
I have in my constituency a lady who inherited some of these perpetual bonds from her father's estate-I hope the hon. member will listen, because I am trying to make a point. In this case they had been held in the family since 1936. According to the strict terms of the hon. member's motion, she would not be eligible because she inherited the bonds from her father. I suggest that is not the criterion which should be used. I do not know how much of the original $55 million issue would be in the hands of the original purchasers, but I doubt it would be more than $5 million to $10 million. I think this bill is based on too narrow a concept. Having inherited from one's father's estate and kept oneself during the years should qualify just as much as being an original purchaser.
I think there are other situations closely akin to this. I am going to get a telephone call tomorrow from this lady, I am sure, when she reads today's Hansard because she has called my attention to this inequitable situation persistently over a long period of time. I can only say to her that I am willing to do everything I can as a member of this place to try to correct something which I believe is wrong.
What is the solution that should be adopted, Mr. Speaker? I do not know how a government can freeze prices in a free market. Either the government redeems or it does not redeem. It seems to me that the government should redeem at face value the debentures of those wlio have demonstrated that they have held them for a certain period of time-I suggest ten years would be sufficient. If purchasers could demonstrate they had owned this security in their own personal title for a period in excess of ten years, I would say that would be good and sufficient grounds for redeeming the debenture.
The question of speculation is a very serious one. In every previous debate on this subject in the House, those who spoke on behalf of the government have said, "Think of all the speculative gains that are going to be made; think of all the banks, those terrible creatures, that will gain; think of the insurance companies that bought on speculation; think of the professional speculators, how terrible it would be if they were to make a dollar out of this sort of thing".
I agree that the speculators should be taken out of the game, but surely the most reasonable way of dealing with the speculator is to establish for those who have not held the securities for the required minimum period a date at which the government would be prepared to go on to the open market and purchase. There is nothing wrong with the concept each year of having something equivalent to a sinking fund for purchasing a certain proportion of the issue that is outstanding. The price at which the government would take the issue off the market would be raised a little to reflect interest, and at a certain date all of it would be retired. I think the date of
February 28, 1977

1996 is ridiculous; I think it should be something like 1986, or at least ten years sooner than 1996.
If the government were to accept the suggestion that 1 am making today-I am sure 1 can convince the hon. member who moved this motion that this makes sense-first to redeem at face value in the case of anyone who could prove continuous ownership in excess of ten years; second, to establish a price at which the government would go on to the open market and purchase offerings, which purchase would be the discounted value of, say, face value in 1986 or some date like that, retiring the issue in an orderly way between now and then, it seems to me that this woul^l meet all of the criteria the hon. member has in mind. First, there would be some equity to the longterm holders who purchased in good faith; secondly, there would be protection against those who purchased for speculative purposes. I agree no one should make a windfall gain out of this, but I think people are entitled to get their money back on some kind of equitable basis.
The incredible thing about this, Mr. Speaker, is the government's reluctance to move. I do not believe it is the government but rather a few senior civil servants who are giving this advice. It is such a picayune item in the total handling of the government's debt. This issue could be retired, I suspect, over a period of years for something like $30 million to $40 million, and the handling of this part of the government's debt is absolutely nothing in terms of debt management. What is at stake here is surely a question of good faith. What is at stake is the assurance to those who purchased government securities that the government is not going to be a hard-nosed private bargainer. The government is in a position of being more than a private bargainer; the government sets the rules of the whole game-the financial market, management of the currency, and the whole question of the degree to which the currency retains its value. The government can influence all of this.
As was argued very ably by the hon. member who proposed the motion, it seems to me that the government has the responsibility of saying to those men and women who bought its securities that while there is no perfect equity in the business market-there are good deals, bad deals; caveat emptor, you take your choice-beyond a certain point the government is going to play fair. Beyond a certain point the government is going to recognize that what has been done was a very serious inequity to those small numbers of people who tried to do the fair, the right, and the honourable thing, as they saw it, and let the government have the use of their funds as part of the government debt.
I think it would be a little easier for the government to be credible if it did this, because in the period ahead it is highly likely that we will have to call upon Canadians for levels of savings and investment in different types of securities. Canada Savings Bonds have, of course, been made extremely attractive, and do not deserve to be mentioned in the same breath as perpetuals. If the government is to maintain its credibility to its citizens and encourage a positive program of savings and investment in government securities, it is an article of faith with me that the government must do something a little better
Perpetual Bonds
for that group of citizens who bought 3 per cent perpetuals, especially for those who have held on to them during difficult times.

A popular move. A great deal has been said on this subject and I am happy to say a few words, partly to learn a few things about the subject that I did not know before, in the hope that it will be resolved once and for all and we will not have concerned elderly people worrying about what is going to happen.
In my short experience with perpetual bonds I have discovered that most of our predecessors who have spoken on the subject have regarded them with some amusement, saying "Oh, that old thing again, the good old perpetual bonds". At the same time, I think it is a fair impression that these bonds have been of real benefit to Canadians over the years. However, their day seems to have come. The history going back to 1936 was well covered by the previous speakers. As well as the original provision for calling these bonds, such as 60 days' notice, some provision to call them by lot is necessary if only some of the bonds were called, and also some measure to try to protect the bond holders.
As we know, in September of 1966 new bond certificates were issued for 30 years. To go back in history, these bonds have had their ups and downs in market value, but mostly down. Apparently the bonds did go up a little after the war, but that was for a very brief time. Within recent years, interest rates in Canada and elsewhere have risen to higher levels. This

February 28, 1977
Perpetual Bonds
has made them rather unpopular in terms of the lower interest rates which originally applied.
With regard to the motion moved by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies), it seems to me that one important aspect is the problem of the distribution of bond holders. That seems to be a very complicated proposition at the moment. However, if we can say one brief thing about that, there seems to have been a substantial change in ownership of the registered bonds since 1966. Since 1936 that change in ownership has been almost complete, so perhaps this mitigates a little the concern for the older bond holders not making it to the final date of 1996.
I understand also that there is some concern about there being a difficulty for the taxpayer in the proposal before us. The government has had a great deal of advantage from having these funds over the years, but it is considered somewhat difficult to ask the taxpayers-many of whom do not have investments of any kind, such as bonds and others-to bear additional interest costs in order to benefit those investors who bought bonds on their own initiative way back in 1936 and since then. It is even more difficult to justify the fortuitous benefit that would be derived by the vast majority of present holders with regard to the change in ownership that I just mentioned.
From the government side, how practical is the motion put forward by the hon. member for Don Valley? There are a number of concerns on the government side. First, there is the problem of trying to identify the original purchasers. Second, there is some problem with discrimination in the proof of purchase. There are problems concerning those bond holders who are deceased and the role of the successors in holding the bonds. There is a problem with selling recently at a loss, which would occur with some people. There is the problem with the proof of ownership once it has been discarded. It would discriminate against those people and would be in favour of those who maintain their ownership. There are various problems with redeeming prices below par.
Apparently various governments have looked at this possibility from time to time. The hon. member for Don Valley mentioned that the United Kingdom has gone very heavily into this type of investment as part of its debt structure, and there are others. The conclusion that has been reached by most of them has been that it would not be in the nation's best interest to fix the maturity date on these obligations.
There is also a concern about setting a rather difficult precedent, an implication that once we take some action to protect the investors from the vagaries of the market there is some discrimination against all other investors. Contrary to what some would propose, this does not apply to the issue of Canada Savings Bonds.
Therefore we have come down to the present solution proposed by the government, which is this. Having regard to all the circumstances, and although not necessarily to the current advantage of taxpayers, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) announced on March 18, 1975, that the 1936 issue of perpetual bonds would be redeemed at par on September 15,

1996. The legal process will be completed by June 7, at which time the Government of Canada will be irrevocably committed by law to redeem the bonds in 1996. Prior to the announcement the bonds were quoted at $37.25 per $100 for a yield of 8 per cent in perpetuity. At the present time the bonds are trading at a price of about $50.75 for a yield of 8.02 per cent to maturity. This yield is now comparable with other long term Government of Canada marketable issues.

these bonds has opened up room for speculation. That is my quarrel with the suggestion of the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) that there be a 1986 date. Any more dates down the road, 1 think, will produce further shifts in the ownership of the bonds and create a further opportunity for speculation. I think the time to settle it is right now.

subtopic: PERPETUAL BONDS, 1936 SUGGESTED REDEMPTION BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
I do not understand it. I asked for some assistance from officials in the Department of Finance. I take it from the hon. member's unwillingness to give an explanation that there is none. Why would we want to freeze the market value of bonds that are going to be redeemed if this resolution is adopted?
I indicated that to understand the equities of perpetual bonds one has to go back over the whole story which began in 1936 when the government of Canada issued $55 million of 3 per cent perpetual bonds at a price of $96.50 to produce a yield to first purchasers of 3.11 per cent in perpetuity. The issue was offered for cash as well as in exchange at par value to holders of a certain series of four year bonds maturing in 1936. A total of $11.3 million in bonds of a total issue of $55 million were issued in exchange for maturing bonds, and the balance was presumably purchased for cash.
The original certificates for the $55 million of bonds bore coupons providing for semi-annual interest. There were 30 years of coupon forms attached to the original bonds so that the last of the coupons would be payable on September 15, 1966. In 1936 the 3 per cent yield was considered relatively attractive because it provided a perpetual annuity on reasonable terms, so as a result it was broadly distributed. That was the first occasion and, I believe, the only occasion on which the government of Canada issued perpetual bonds. But there was a pattern of perpetual bonds, Mr. Speaker. They were an understandable security throughout the world of bonds. Similar bonds have long been an important part of the debt structure of the United Kingdom, and the hon. member for Don Valley aknowledged this. It was not some novel security never heard of before, but was well known in many countries. In 1935 about 60 per cent of the marketable outstanding debt of Great Britain was in the form of perpetual or undated bonds called consols.
The 1936 issue included a provision that the bonds could be called in whole or in part on 60 days' notice by the government at par any time after September 15, 1966, the date of the last coupon. If less than all the bonds were called by the government then the bonds to be redeemed would be determined by lot. Again, this call provision in a government perpetual security was a common feature of long maturity bonds issued by
Perpetual Bonds
enterprises in the private sector. On the one hand, such a feature is intended to protect the bondholders from having their bonds called prior to the call date. This prevents the issuer from calling the bonds during periods of lower interest rates and refinancing them with bonds offering a lower yield.
In the case of the 1936 issue, the 30-year period did provide protection to the holders on those occasions when the bonds traded at prices exceeding the issue price. There were periods when they did trade at values in excess of the issue price. On the other hand, the right of the issuer to call provides protection to the country's taxpayers by permitting the bonds to be called subsequent to the call date should lower interest rate levels permit them to be refunded and replaced by lower cost debt. The 30-year call provision is therefore a trade-off between the interests of the lender and the borrower and, together with yield, constitute the basic determinants of the market value of a security of any given term. In September, 1966, new bond certificates were issued, with an additional supply of coupons attached sufficient for an additional 30 years. They replaced the 30-year-old bond certificates.
The perpetual bonds are marketable and their price is therefore determined by the play of market forces. Since they were issued, their market price has generally lected changing levels of interest rates in Canada. For se._.al years after the war the market price exceeded the issue price and, consequently, sellers of the bonds at that time could have and did obtain a capital gain. Within recent years interest rates in Canada and elsewhere have risen to much higher levels and the market prices of perpetual bonds, as for the vast majority of fixed interest obligations everywhere-I include government fixed rate obligations and fixed interest obligations issued by private sector enterprises-have, as a consequence, declined substantially below their issue prices.
At the end of 1976 about 45 per cent of perpetual bonds were held in bearer form. It is impossible to determine with any degree of precision which of these holders bought the bonds at the original purchase price, or at prices higher than the current market price. However, the balance of $30 million worth of bonds were held, at first issue, in registered form.
At my request the Department of Finance tracked down about half the number of bonds issued, namely, the registered bonds. They were held by 3,575 investors. Today, 1.3 per cent are held by investors who purchased the bonds at the time of issue in 1936. Those untransferred bonds are held by 109 investors, three of whom hold 60 per cent of the $379,000. Therefore part (a) of the motion, which calls for original purchasers to receive the full face value for their bonds, will apply to only 1.3 per cent of the total value of the issue. We are considering only the original bonds issued in registered form. Clearly, we are talking about a small amount of money. The hon. member is right. And we are talking about 109 people, a relatively small group.
Let us assume that the unregistered bonds have been held more or less in the same ratio. That would mean that we are

February 28, 1977
Perpetual Bonds
talking about, say, 200 people who have retained their bonds from 1936. Their bond issues would now be valued at, say, about $750,000. The hon. member wants to call our attention to the injustices suffered by those who have had to hold their bonds for such a long time. Naturally, bonds not held by the original issuees have been sold to others. Some of those buyers bought at prices higher than face value, and others may have bought at below face value. The motion goes on to call on the government to repay the difference to bond holders.
The trouble with the motion is that it only calls for justice for those who presently hold those bonds. If you are putting the case on equitable grounds you must ask, are the equities greater for those who still hold those bonds, that is, for those who bought them on the date of issue or bought them subsequently, or for those who sold the bonds? The question arises, should one feel more sorry for those who have held the bonds all this time, or bought them within ten or 15 years of issue, when the price was not the same as the present price, or should one feel more sorry for those who took big losses?
The hon. member for Don Valley in referring to those people acknowledged that they had probably taken big losses. But he spoke of people who still have those bonds in their portfolios. Perhaps the people who were forced to sell did not have portfolios. Perhaps they had to sell because they needed the money, not for investing but for living. If you want to approach this issue on equitable grounds, would you not also want to hear from those who had to sell their bonds over the years and were forced to take less than they paid? The motion says, nothing about that group'. If I were to guess, 1 would say that that group of people might be far worse off, having suffered more from inflation, than the group which presently holds the bonds and to whose cause the hon. member has been recruited.
There is a broader issue to consider. The hon. member's motion calls for justice for one small group of people hurt by inflation. But many people in this country have been the victims of inflation, and they have not all been victims at the hands of the government-if I can put it that way. If the government could write a cheque, to redeem the damage done by inflation, that cheque would have to be for an extraordinarily large amount. The victims of inflation tend to be the aged, tend to be those on fixed incomes, tend to be the poor. If we are to begin remedying injustices and compensating for inflation, does the hon. member suggest we should begin with bond holders? Perhaps we should take the amount of money involved-whatever it is-and compensate for inflation by helping those in society who are the worst off. I know the hon. member would agree with me when I say that the bond holders in Canada, the holder of government securities, are not usually among the worst off. I could refer to many existing programs of the government which fight inflation and seek to compensate its victims.
