subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned the debate on Bill C-27 at five o'clock, I was speaking about the mobility of workers.
When employment conditions generally worsened in 1970, the migration responses to differences in income prospects became less significant, and the short-term income increases experienced by migrants became less favourable. Of course, while the migrant may benefit marginally from the move, the migration process contributes in a minor way to the structural problem.
When an unemployed person leaves a region, he takes with him his expenditures on locally produced goods and services, which to a large extent is financed from federal transfer funds such as unemployment insurance and general welfare payments. Through the multiplier process, his reduction in expenditures produces an unfavourable effect on the sending region's employment.
Under the new phase schedule, this effect might be mitigated by compensating for high unemployment. Regions with unemployment rates near, or slightly above, the national average will be much better off, whereas places like Vancouver and Victoria would receive only eight weeks of national extended entitlement and receive no regional extended entitlement under the present system. The three-phase schedule would grant these regions 14 to 20 weeks of regional extended benefits in those circumstances where the national rate is 8 per cent.
February 28, 1977

I am skeptical, at best, about regional adjustments wherein unemployment figures are compared to the national average. The example of the Canada Works allocation in my riding and the fiasco surrounding the additional allocations for materials, have not endeared me to the government's generosity. Regional manpower figures certainly do not jive with those used as criteria for eligibility; but then the minister has assured me that "other factors were used".
That specific criticism aside, 1 wonder about the wisdom and intent of using 8 per cent unemployment as a benchmark for computing benefits and schedules. While this does not seem overly optimistic on the government's behalf, 1 suppose it is only realistic. Faced with the possibility of such a rate, the government must consider the ramifications. The financial impact of the new three-phase benefit structure at that rate will be, unfortunately, minimal. The logical course then is not only to try to minimize the losses, as this proposal thankfully does, but to attack the source of the problem-a sagging economy.
We know, for instance, that the pulp and paper industry is suffering. Sales started to recover in early 1976, but by mid-year demand was dropping. There was a price increase announced for July 1, 1976, and publishing companies responded by placing large orders early in the year and were fully stocked before the increases took effect. So we need new markets.
The construction industry association in British Columbia has indicated that, while there is no shortage of workers, the level of construction by private enterprise will be very low this year. This raises the cost of housing. Paradoxically, a high cost of housing is translated by the Department of Manpower as a sign of a healthy regional economy and disqualifies a riding from Canada Works funds. So less jobs are created, the price goes up even further, and on and on until about 21 per cent of union carpenters and labourers across British Columbia are collecting unemployment insurance. The government might suggest work sharing to ensure that their incomes be higher than U.I. benefits and that they don't lose their skills. The unions don't look too favourably on the idea, and seniority tends to affect the sharing scheme.
Fortunately, I can speak today with the benefit of the findings of the comprehensive review of the unemployment insurance program in Canada tabled earlier. It suggested further areas of study which I find to be the real crux of the issue and which the government has not had the courage to approach.
The extent to which the unemployment insurance program facilitates productive job search and speed in return of unemployed persons to productive employment relevant to their skills was one area. It cannot be argued that we do not need a program to insure against temporary loss or wages. But disincentives to work are inherent in the scheme, and the lack of an effective job creation and job search program only aggravates the situation. The labour force experience of the covered
Employment and Immigration
population has to be monitored. A more ambitious analysis of claimant behaviour before, during, and after a claim is necessary to evaluate the effects of the U.I.C. program in meeting its twin objectives of providing adequate income replacement and helping workers to a rewarding and stable employment.
After all, the effectiveness of the U.I.C. program depends on government's over-all social and economic policies and, in particular, on manpower policies and programs. We need policies to alleviate the problems, not some mechanical reaction to statistical quotations and budget estimates. We have to re-appraise the unemployment insurance, not only because it is costing too much but, because it is the wrong approach, it is a defensive reaction rather than an offensive assault on unemployment itself.
It is inhumane to threaten Canadians, to threaten to cut them off insurance benefits without promising to engage in job creation programs. It is demoralizing and damaging to the work ethic to charge so many Canadians with what amounts to fraud. We on this side of the House are the first to admit that there are rip-offs but these can and are being controlled at the administrative level. What we should be discussing, what we should be planning, are alternatives to unemployment, not alternatives to the insurance scheme.
It is frustrating for unemployed Canadians that nothing is being done. It is doubly frustrating for young Canadians contemplating post-secondary education to know, before they begin, that chances are poor of having the opportunity to apply their acquired talents. Those individuals have to be encouraged. We can't cop out on them now. They need and should be rewarded with a new budget which takes into consideration all the ills of our economic environment, and that addresses itself to these by providing stimulants. We need sales tax cuts and promotions for the housing industry. Industries should be encouraged to reinstate research and development programs. They should also be encouraged to locate in areas where unemployment is at its highest.
These approaches would cost, in the long run, less than trying to support close to a million people on transfer payments, because employment not only reduces the cost of the insurance scheme, it helps the economy get rolling again. Instead, we know that new capital investment will be down in Canada this year. We have to make every effort to recreate a climate of confidence in Canada or we will continue to see the great potential of this country wasted.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the introduction of this legislation is certainly timely, if only because it gives us an opportunity to discuss the unemployment insurance program, something which has become a major factor in our economy and, indeed, in our performance around the world.
I thought there were significant implications contained in the comprehensive review of the unemployment insurance program tabled in the House. It drew attention to the fact that expenditures on unemployment insurance are the equivalent of about 10 per cent of the total federal budget and 2.1 per cent of the gross national product. It is evident that the over-all

February 28, 1977
Employment and Immigration
economic and social impact of the program can hardly be underestimated, and its administration is of corresponding importance.
Unemployment insurance has come a long way since the thirties when the concept was to provide some sort of basic insurance against unemployment. While in its earlier days the provisions of the act constituted, for the most part, a true insurance program, the present act is obviously filled with items such as income maintenance, social welfare and other benefits, including "job creation" and so on.
With the bill before us, the government is putting a few patches on the act, proposing, among other things, that 50,000 people should be cut off the unemployment insurance rolls at a saving to the government of $110 million a year. The cost of the program today has certainly escalated since the days when Mackenzie King first introduced it. The estimate, then, was $70 million a year, whereas now the scheme runs through $70 million in a week and a half. Over the years a great deal of welfarism has crept in, the most obvious example being the provision for insuring groups with intermittent employment opportunities, for example, fishermen who, being selfemployed, should not have been covered on any insurance basis. There is no doubt that fishermen should have a program available to them, but it would not be easy, as I understand fishermen, for them to be covered by an insurance program. I understand from conversations with many maritimers that if the fishermen were covered by some other program the statistics would not be nearly as bad, and the assessment of programs could be made on a sounder basis.
These new costs sent the fund into bankruptcy in the 1960's. The Gill Commission suggested that the fund be restricted to insurance purposes and further proposed that everyone, not just groups at risk, should be called upon to pay for coverage. The extension of coverage along these lines was obviously an important feature of Mr. Mackasey's reform of unemployment insurance in 1971.
Presumably Mr. Mackasey believed his new system was sacred. It has already been tinkered with. Last year people over 65 were dropped from the rolls. In addition the federal treasury was relieved of $600 million which was transferred, through a pay roll tax, to employers and employees. This year it is proposed to chop at the other end. People who work for less than 12 weeks may not claim benefits. This, I might point out, is in itself a departure from the insurance principle. The government takes money from these people, through deductions, and gives nothing back.
The diverting of money from the fund to a work sharing scheme is certainly not part of the insurance principle. No plan will ever be perfect, but the most serious criticism of the attempt to reform the unemployment insurance system is that it still leaves an element of welfare where needs are financed by a regressive tax which tends to hit the low income people harder than those of high income.

The changes last year concerning the moving average system of deductions increases the employer-employee share to a higher and higher level, so that eventually the whole system will be borne by the employer-employee and the cost to the federal treasury will diminish to nothing. Indeed the thought arises that deductions would be so great that a system of contract might even replace wages, which seems to have been happening. I think this is an important observation because, since the government is going to transfer money to certain groups for a scheme, the cost of which is entirely borne by the employer and employee, with the government not putting in any money of its own, we could be in serious difficulties.
As a parliamentarian, and having observed the workings of unemployment insurance in 1971, in my opinion two main things have happened. The first was that the benefits were greatly increased over their pre-1971 level. As I recall, the level of benefits in 1971 was approximately 41 per cent of the average weekly wage, with many benefits as low as 30 per cent. The highest was slightly over 50 per cent, but even then the individual had to be in the low income brackets and have numerous dependants. Since the 1971 legislation it has been obvious that the program has shifted drastically from the insurance principle to income transfer, through the combination of welfare coverage, greater benefit entitlement, and federally financed extended benefits.
As the comprehensive review of the unemployment insurance program asks, should unemployment insurance play an increasing role in the redistribution of total income maintenance and in the government's over-all social and economic policies? In other words, should only those parts of the country that have a strong economy support those regions that have a weak economy? Certainly this is happening at the present time. Does this practice over a period of time merely perpetuate discrepancies and allow individuals to have as good a living and standard of care in one part of the country as in another, particularly when substantial groups of people do not need to work compared with those living in other parts of the country?
A study of the relationship between cost and employer-employee benefits and deductions shows many interesting things. For example, in 1974, the last year for which I have figures, citizens of Newfoundland received benefits of $114 million, with deductions of $26 million. Nova Scotia received benefits of $93 million, with deductions of $50 million. New Brunswick received benefits of $105 million, with deductions of $39 million. Quebec received benefits of $740 million, with deductions of $408 million. Ontario received benefits of $609 million, with deductions of $669 million. Manitoba received benefits of $49 million, with deductions of $71 million. Saskatchewan received benefits of $46 million, with deductions of $44 million. Alberta received $66 million, with deductions of $123 million. British Columbia received benefits of $281 million, with deductions of $178 million. Total benefits paid were $2,115 million, while deductions collected were $1,600 million. With an additional cost of $150 million for administration, the total cost of the plan was almost $2,300 million. In other
February 28, 1977

words, $700 million had to come from the federal treasury, or out of general revenue.
Assuming that citizens in all parts of Canada paid approximately the same in tax, it is obvious that there has been a shift of money out of the prairies and Ontario to Quebec and the maritime provinces, while British Columbia broke about even. As one who comes from the prairies, I know there are many people in my area who leave for greater opportunities in British Columbia, where wages are considerably better and work opportunities greater. In short, in a province with primarily a high agricultural base, a number of its working force do quite poorly in terms of benefiting from unemployment insurance. They have to pay large amounts toward general tax revenue, but since they are a self-employed group they are not able to partake of the many benefits of the plan.
The review discusses the fundamental alienation of adequate income protection and work disincentives, and I think this is the central core of the whole program. All members will remember the large number of claims that were brought to their attention once the new act was introduced. I am sure many hoped, as I did, that as the program began to work itself out calls on individual members would settle down into some kind of regular pattern. This, in my experience, has not happened, and I think it has not happened because of the definition in the act that, in order to collect benefits, a claimant must be actively seeking work. Obviously this condition is very difficult to define, especially in rural areas.
Many people in my area have been cut off unemployment insurance because, in the eyes of the unemployment insurance officer, they did not have adequate transportation. Immediate job opportunities are often sparse in rural areas. The question arises whether or not rural workers are not disadvantaged, as it is much more difficult for them to prove they are looking for work than it is for those who live in cities.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I have been struck by the fact that I have little trouble with workers who belong to large corporations or large unions. These people seem to have a much easier time proving eligibility for unemployment insurance than those who work in less organized industries, particularly casual workers on farms, small company employees and so on. Where a claimant receives benefits it is, in large measure, a kind of lottery in that one has to make the right answers on the right form.
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, the decision on whether an individual receives unemployment insurance rests with the unemployment insurance officer. With this in mind, the amount of money paid out by the UIC depends on what a specific officer thinks of a specific application. I think this is the weakness of the plan. It does not appear to be fair and is not fair to many recipients.
There is no doubt that there is a large element of cynicism about who should receive benefits. The tribunal that was set up to guard against this does not seem to be very effective. In the past I advised applicants in my riding to appear before the tribunal to state their case, even though they may have had to travel 200 or 300 miles to do so. Judging from the actions of
Employment and Immigration
the tribunal, in my opinion they have always supported the unemployment insurance officer; as a result, I have quit advising people to make the journey because it is almost certain that the tribunal will find against them. Indeed the tribunal seems to go out of its way to make things difficult in some instances. For example, claimants have received a notice to appear after the date that was set for the hearing. In fact tribunals have themselves been doing their bit to clamp down on unemployment insurance by virtually always agreeing with the unemployment insurance officer.
Another important aspect is what effect unemployment insurance has on the work ethic, job attentiveness, and so on.
We hear much about the fact that people should have rewarding and fulfilling jobs, whatever that may be. Much of this would indicate that the necessity to work is not related to productivity or to doing a job that society finds useful. In effect most jobs are boring and unrewarding to the spirit, but there is little we can do about it. Life is like that. During the war an army selection group was supposed to put the square pegs in the square holes and the round pegs in the round holes, but as the war progressed people could neither be placed in positions they wanted nor could positions be found to suit them. At one time 90 per cent of the men had to go into the infantry because that is where the losses were the greatest.
When you consider Table C-5 of the comprehensive review which indicates that work shortages accounted for only 27 per cent of the lay-offs while voluntary separations amounted to 41 per cent, it is certainly interesting to note that of most people who quit their jobs only 25 per cent did so due to lack of work. The table also indicates that of those who quit voluntarily many did not make claims.
There are some interesting comments on disqualifications and disentitlement, one of them being that females have a significantly higher incidence of disqualification and disentitlement than males, regardless of insured weeks or dependency status. In other words, it appears they quit their jobs without any just cause in the eyes of UIC.
In Table C-15 there is a most significant factor in assessing the over-all effect on unemployment insurance. It indicates that only 26.8 per cent of males who received benefits had dependants, while 37 per cent who received benefits had no dependants. This was also significant with regard to females. Only 1.7 per cent of females who received benefits had dependants, while 34 per cent who received benefits had no dependants. In other words, of the total number of claimants, 71.5 per cent were single-or at least had no dependants. Further statistics showed that there was a significantly larger number of claimants under 25 years of age than people of that age in the work force, which is to be expected.
All of these facts should be a lesson to us, or at least an assessment of the way in which things are going. If only 27 per cent of job separations are due to shortage of work-and 1 doubt the number is that high because certainly most private employers, even when the job separation is voluntary, make
3498

February 28, 1977
Employment and Immigration
out certificates indicating that there is no work available in order to enable the claimant to make his claim earlier-it certainly seems significant that almost 72 per cent of the claimants are single so far as the income tax is concerned. In other words, these single people in the labour force-at least single so far as income tax is concerned-did not worry too much about job separation and must have left their jobs because of personal reasons, unlike those who have dependants.
The question arises that if 66% per cent of the average weekly wage is not too great a sum for single people-at least if we are to maintain the spirit of the UIC Act-then 1 believe that the crux of the problem is the benefits obtained by single people under this legislation. In fact in a country with our cold climate, if an unemployed person is to receive 66% per cent of his wage in unemployment insurance benefits, there is some truth in supposing that many would consider themselves as well off not working, especially when the job entails working outside in cold weather, buying expensive clothes and working in unpleasant conditions. There are also complications with cars which refuse to start in cold weather, and other such difficulties resulting from the cold climate. We are all entitled in a free society to make the best we can in the circumstances, and I imagine that there are always some people in any society who arrange things in such a way that they do not have to work as hard as their fellow workers. No one, least of all myself, disagrees with their right to do this, but I think the question is whether or not they should receive equal remuneration for less work.
Another area that brings unemployment insurance into disrepute is the fact that the program makes little allowance for the dollars earned in any one year. With wages as high as they are now, particularly in certain industries, in a few months a person can earn $10,000 to $20,000 and yet draw unemployment insurance for a substantial portion of the year. Meanwhile there are many people who toil for a much smaller total yearly return, who are never unemployed, and who never draw unemployment insurance benefits. These people become very discouraged and resentful because they feel the system to be inequitable when deductions from their wages go to pay unemployment benefits to people who make a great deal more money than they themselves do because their jobs are seasonal.
Unemployment benefits should certainly be related to the total yearly earnings, and perhaps methods should be considered whereby the unemployed, particularly those in lower income groups, could have their deductions reduced or eliminated if they are unemployed for a number of years.
In my opinion benefits amounting to 66% per cent of the previous wages are too high for claimants with no dependants. I think a good case can be made for claimants with dependants receiving this percentage of wages. I believe there is substantial evidence that when benefits amount to more than 50 per cent there is an abnormal call on the benefit structure. This is certainly true in the case of unemployment insurance related to job separations of many millions of people. Such a benefit structure plays a large part in encouraging excessive work

changes and separations without just cause, at least causes other than the unavailability of work.
With regard to the change of the eight to 12 weeks 1 have mixed feelings, but certainly I think the old requirement of the eight to 16 weeks was far too generous. However, if a person pays unemployment insurance for eight to 12 weeks and then receives no benefits at all, he or she is unhappy, and it certainly seems unfair that they should not be abie to receive some benefits for their contributions. Certainly they should not be able to receive the extended benefits received by those with a real attachment to the labour force, but it is debatable whether they should have nothing for their deductions.
We should consider the circumstances in our cold climate where much of the work is seasonal, and students are not entitled to benefits because they cannot qualify. This raises an issue which I think should be considered. Some of these people can only work for a few weeks and they will not be able to claim the benefits, so they should have no deductions from their pay.
The effect of this bill will be to reduce the claims on the unemployment insurance fund, but it will certainly not cure all the problems. The allocation of moneys for the partial payment of wages does not seem to be in keeping with the insurance principle. It does not attack the problem in the benefit structure which seems to encourage unemployment, particularly in the younger age group. On the national level it seems to create the problem in that regions with a high unemployment rate continue to have that high rate of unemployment. Furthermore, job mobility from one region to another will not be discouraged by high unemployment insurance benefits.
It might be wise for the government to bring forward some statistics along the lines produced in the comprehensive review showing whether or not job mobility from one region to another is being discouraged by high unemployment benefits and, if so, to what degree. There are still a good many unanswered questions in this legislation, and I hope the minister will provide some answers in committee.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that when this government wants to sell a rather shoddy or questionable product it usually tries to package it together with some good which, at least apparently, looks more palatable. That is how I feel about Bill C-27, establishing the department of employment and immigration, the Canada employment and immigration commission and the Canada employment and immigration advisory council; a department, a commission, a council, it looks merely like a rearrangement of already existing institutions.
If all this commotion, this jumble of re-definition of terms of reference and structures, on both national and regional levels, were really to do some good to the country, 1 would certainly support the bill. Of course, a small army of officials has already spent a long time studying this issue. Some well-paid
February 28, 1977

officials would have been more productive trying to solve our present problems instead of devising new structures which would clear up all difficulties. However, I would take a chance to support this part of the bill, not without strong reservation. I shall return to this later on if I have time.
For the moment, I want to come back to my preliminary comments on the title of the bill dealing with the reorganization of government services and also with the working labour force and is aimed at amending the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1971. It is on that part of the bill that I wish to make a few comments. It is also to that part of the bill that I referred at the beginning, when I spoke about a shoddy product packaged with a palatable added as an appendix to be shaken off.
Everyone in the House knows that there are some people in this country-and by this I mean employers-who openly condemn unemployment insurance and pay wages which hardly reach provincial minimum wages. For such employers, the removal of unemployment insurance would be just like giving them carte blanche to take unfair advantage of a captive and poor labour force ignorant of their rights and the legislation. There is also another group of employers who can live with the Unemployment Insurance Act, but only to a certain extent.
The law allows them to make the best of difficult situations, generally to their advantage and at the expense of the employee. It is a way for those employers to get their activities subsidized. It is also a convenient way to free themselves of their social responsibilities and to pretend at the same time that they have a social conscience. That kind of employer consciously takes advantage of the system, and let nobody try to have me believe that only workers abuse the unemployment insurance syste'm, when there are abuses.
The kind of employers I am referring to often take advantage of a slow period or a temporary or seasonal decrease of activity to lay off employees they should keep come rain or come shine. Those people simply say: "Society will take care of them, if they just apply for unemployment insurance." That is the reaction of those masters with little conscience.
I should point out that those two types of employers, that is the one who rejects unemployment insurance totally, and the other who accepts it because of the egotistical advantages the system provides for business and profits, those two types of employers can go into the same bag. Both refuse to recognize the right of their employees to organize into unions to protect their interests and will lay off any employee of theirs who talks about labour association. And it is not suprising that the employers of this type are found very often in areas of generally high unemployment. I could state names, but I shall not take advantage of my privileges as a member of the House to do so. However, I shall mention them outside when the time comes, Mr. Speaker, as I have already started to do.
And yet, when do we hear about these bad employers who abuse the system? Most of the time we hear about the small wage earner who can neither defend himself nor make use of the media to present his views. Apparently it is better not to
Employment and Immigration
mention these bad employers who hurt small wage earners who are defenceless.
If I have mentioned these two cases, Mr. Speaker, it is because I want to get rid once and for all of all these stories about workers who are supposedly taking the system for a ride. It is unfair on the part of the news media to spread these stories and to make generalization from exceptional cases. Rather, let us talk about employers who force some of their employees into ambiguous situations where often the weakness of human nature prevails.
It is unfortunate to use this bill to reduce the revenue of the poor, for such is the effect that this bill will eventually have. And at this very moment, Mr. Speaker, most of the workers do not realize all the implications of this bill. They do not realize that they will be the victims three months, six months, two years from now whenever this bill will be enacted, if ever.
I do not like this legislation and I say so quite frankly, I do not like it being introduced along with a measure of administrative reorganization. I can support the first part, which is not perfect but which has undoubtedly become necessary because of the defects in the old organization and particularly because of the lack of integrated services to the working force over the years.
Last Thursday evening, while driving home, I listened to a review of the area press in the Atlantic provinces. It was a CBC broadcast and the commentator who was reviewing some press reports said at one point that the government had been forced to amend the UIC Act to calm down the outcry raised particularly in Ontario during the last general election.
I cannot believe, Mr. Speaker, that this is so. Oh, we all heard those self-righteous voices during the last general election as well as during the previous one asking the federal government to cut down unemployment insurance and force the people to go to work. If this is the situation the commentator was referring to last week, he was probably right in guessing that the government simply wanted to improve its electoral position with an eye to the next general election, but never would I believe that measures that have proved beneficial until now and have dealt with a situation in our economy that had to be corrected as it has been since would be abandoned.
I warn hon. members from Ontario, the province from which rose the outcry. Regardless of the side of the House on which they sit, it seems to me it is their duty to explain to their electors-and perhaps I could make the same request of hon. members who come from more privileged areas in Canada- that there are areas in Canada whose rate of growth is still lower than the national rate. It is also their duty, as I see it, to counterbalance what the press reports about the few persons who abused the unemployment insurance system. Is that any reason to punish everyone by reducing, across the board the number of weeks giving entitlement and benefits? To my mind, that is a blow to the poor worker who cannot defend himself.
3500

February 28, 1977
Employment and Immigration
It is difficult for city dwellers-and in this, I am not making a personal reference to the colleague who sits across from me this evening-but it seems to me it is difficult for people who come either from Forestville or Westmount to understand or try to imagine the situation a family head, father or mother, without work, as there are some now in my riding of Mada-waska-Victoria where a number of work activities producing employment depend essentially on the seasons, and where the difference between work and unemployment depends on outside factors and decisions more often than otherwise than on the will to work of my elector.
As several hon. members said before, it is not a matter of working when we feel like it and then taking holidays at the expense of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. When there is work in Madawaska-Victoria, people work! They are eager to work! Whole families, for generations, have gone into exile in the United States to respect their right to work, to earn the daily bread on their table, to feed their children and send them to school. And even today, in my province of New Brunswick, many citizens leave their city, their town, on Sunday night, to go and work in Saint John, in New Brunswick, and come back home late on Friday night or early Saturday morning.
Those people want to work, they go where they can find work. However, there are limits, Mr. Speaker; some people cannot travel. Some people have too many local obligations to be able to sacrifice everything to a rather temporary job. Unfortunately no mention is made of such situations.
There is very little industrial decentralization in favour of underdeveloped areas in spite of the considerable effort made by the present federal administration which provides for loans without interest, subsidies for manpower training and many other programs. Indeed the government decided a bit late to decentralize their own operations, which is an excellent move. Far be it from me to try to minimize the important part played by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion since 1969. I give them very high marks because they tried to improve the regional economy of the Atlantic provinces in particular. However, I give the highest mark to those industrialists in the Atlantic region who took full advantage of the DREE programs to create temporary and permanent jobs in our part of Canada. But I have yet to see, except for some very rare exceptions, the private sector of central Canada, of the very prosperous city of Toronto for instance, send us industries and take advantage of the benefits offered by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion.
I am quite aware, Mr. Speaker, that we are discussing the unemployment insurance plan and the reorganizing of federal employment services. Yet, it is difficult not to mention the Department of Regional Economic Expansion in that context, and I seriously wonder if the reorganization went far enough, if some components of the reorganization of the Department of Manpower, as we know it at the present time, would not have made more sense being linked with some of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion whose main task is to create and promote creation of new industries in the Atlantic area.

However, if we have missed the boat this time, we must hope to get on board later on. We must achieve not only a better coordination of components within the Department of Manpower and Immigration and the Unemployment Insurance Commission but also better relations between this and other government departments.
Mr. Speaker, I am not in the mood to support the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act as contained in this bill. Tonight we talk about the principle in general. I deliberately avoided going into details; I hope I will have that opportunity further on at the committee stage or when the bill comes back to the House, if we are not successful in having some amendments passed. Several times in the last few months, I examined that question, not individually but with several of my colleagues, and I must admit quite frankly tonight that I do not have a clear conscience about the bill as it is now presented. I cannot say all I have to say, but I only want to express what I think is the concern of many of my constituents, many citizens from New Brunswick and even from the entire Atlantic region. And I will have the opportunity, as I said earlier, to come back to that matter.

To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer briefly to a fairly thick document received a few weeks ago entitled "Comprehensive Review of the Unemployment Insurance Program in Canada" published by the Unemployment Insurance Commission. This study, said to be the first of its kind, was done with the help of official departmental experts and a number of outside consultants. It is presented as the first major analysis of the impact of unemployment insurance on Canadian society and economy.
The study is, if I may say so, rather non-conclusive in many of its conclusions. One of the statements which has drawn my particular attention is found in the concluding observations on page L-8, and I quote:
It should be noted that the review did not examine the more beneficial socio-economic impacts of UI, such as maintaining dignity, supporting a skilled job pool, etc.
Goodness knows what they mean by "etc.". It is beyond my comprehension that the document which is presented under the guise of the first major analysis of its kind would leave out such a fundamental concern as the one I have just referred to, that is, "the more beneficial socio-economic impacts of Ul, such as maintaining dignity, supporting a skilled job pool, etc."
It is for these two reasons that I cannot go along with the bill as much as I know of it and as much as I have read about it. Perhaps I am a slow learner. I do not have the legal training of the super experts who have made statements on the bill. In certain respects it is a jungle. Only an experienced lawyer can make his way through the mumbo-jumbo of some of the propositions of the bill. But one thing hits home, openly and directly-the small worker, the small man and his family, will be adversely affected by some of the clauses modifying the Unemployment Insurance Act. I do not like that.
February 28, 1977

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to make a few comments on the legislation before us. At the outset, I would like to say that 1 have followed very closely the speech made by the hon. member for Madawaska (Mr. Corbin) who, in my opinion-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Madawaska-Victoria!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
-Madawaska-Victoria, granted, who, in my opinion, seemed concerned about this legislation. He said that his fellow citizens are also concerned, and I believe that on the government side, there are also other members who are as concerned as he is. I would hope that, like the previous speaker, they will have the courage and the candour to point out to the minister the concerns and dangers involved in this legislation.
It is true that reference is made to restructuration and reorganization. It is also true that this is an experiment, and since this government has made several such experiments in the past decade but not always with the anticipated results, I believe, like the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria and this side of the House, that we have every reason to be concerned and to entertain serious doubts about this new experiment of the government and the minister. Moreover, when considering the bill before us one might well wonder why the government had to introduce such legislation. About two weeks ago, I said in this House that the government was much more willing to introduce social measures than to create jobs, and in view of its numerous failures, I feel we have been very generous towards unemployment insurance and other social measures.
Today we want to apply a certain rigidity, which we did not dare do a few years ago, and as it then seemed to be a makeshift or a short term solution which is now turning into a long-term solution, we are forced to back up to a point where we will embarrass thousands of Canadians. Given this legislation which requires 12 weeks instead of eight for claimants to qualify, it is clear in the present context that the period was never so ill chosen to introduce such a bill.
Perhaps a measure of this kind could have been introduced a few years ago but they waited for years and years. At the very moment when specialists forecast an increase in the rate of unemployment for 1977 we are presented with a legislation that will in effect send thousands of Canadians directly to welfare offices without considering-and perhaps the government thought about it-that the provinces are responsible for the additional expenditures for people they will help financially because they are no longer entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. We believe, of course, as the government does, that work incentives must be put in-we agree on that-but I do not think that the period was well chosen to introduce such a legislation.
And there is absolutely no concern about those areas facing great difficulties with that plague called unemployment.
Employment and Immigration
Thank God, an amendment will be introduced in due time to ask Parliament at least to enforce that minimum qualification period of 12 weeks only in areas where the unemployment rate does not cause too much hardship. We hoped, of course, to have the support of a majority in this House considering that I think this amendment is quite humane and quite logical in view of the economic context in which we find ourselves if we seriously want to avoid the worst from the results of this legislation.
So, as I was saying, Mr. Speaker, in the absence of adequate policies to create jobs, they managed to introduce measures to keep people on unemployment. Indeed, I repeat that the Prime Minister did warn us that we would have to get used to a rate of unemployment that was at the time much lower than it is today. But when we talk of about one million unemployed in this country I seriously wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether that is really the best time to introduce such a legislation. Once again, it seems that the government could not care less about the amount of money the provinces will have to pay to these persons, once they will be on welfare. I think we will find other short-term solutions. One hears of course of all the savings which will be made on the cost of the programs and which will be used to find all kinds of new policies to help raise our productivity and create job training or job creation programs. But, Mr. Speaker, the government has already adopted similar policies through its Canada Manpower Centres with a certain success but this did not prevent unemployment to increase in Canada to the present high level.
I think this is the very moment to invite the minister to weigh seriously the effects that the enforcement of this legislation could have, particularly on the most disadvantaged areas, and when I say disadvantaged 1 mean the areas where the present rate of unemployment is totally unacceptable. To think that all people who draw unemployment insurance benefits are not seeking jobs is totally wrong. In the area 1 represent, I met this morning with some union representatives and I had the opportunity to discuss with them and with journalists who are seriously studying the situation in my constituency where the rate of unemployment seems to be now around 10 to 13 per cent, a rate which we had never seen in this area before. There is a great deal of concern there about this legislation.
1 do not know yet to what extent this legislation now before the House will not be implemented. Under normal conditions, I would be in complete agreement with the minister. If we had a reasonable unemployment rate, I would fully agree with the government. But the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin) referred to the concerns, the dangers and the hardships that such a legislation would cause, and 1 think that we, on this side of the House, have been quite outspoken on this issue.
Are these comments enough to make the minister realize the seriousness of the present situation? All this because the government failed to develop adequate policies and to have enough leadership to prevent us from facing a catastrophe.

February 28, 1977
Employment and Immigration
Unemployment is the main disease of Canada. But once again, we have long said that the government has not had the foresight even to protect Canadian industry, which, in my opinion, if more courageous action had been taken, could have maintained a much lower unemployment rate than the present one.
May I also remind the minister of a flagrant injustice concerning this whole unemployment insurance policy? I want to mention it particularly because the government has already referred to and agreed to rectify an injustice, a monumental mistake that some officials made in December 1975 concerning people aged 65 who were declared ineligible for unemployment insurance benefits during the following year even if they did not find any employment. I would like to note that this concerns a group of people of which nearly 99.9 per cent had seldom received unemployment insurance benefits and who had been most proud and laborious for 40 or 45 years.
The decision made by the government in December 1975 rendered them ineligible for unemployment insurance if they wished to stay in the work force. Of course, when those people lost their entitlement to unemployment benefits and had to rely on their old age security pension, they naturally claimed benefits from their retirement pension plans, whether the Canada Pension Plan or the Quebec Pension Plan. They had no other choice, and since the officials had told them that it was all over, they applied for the Quebec Pension Plan. Recently, after a number of people complained about a vested interest, the government lost this case and it is now obliged to pay unemployment insurance benefits to these people. But in this case, in its own typical way the government has deceived these people of 65, stating that it would pay back only those who have not applied for retirement pension benefits. I know that when you claim benefits under the Quebec Pension Plan or the Canada Pension Plan, you recognize effectively that you no longer wish to work. But it is necessary to remind the House that if those people have applied under a pension plan, it is because they were deceived when they were told they would no longer be entitled to any unemployment insurance benefits.
In a most generous move, the minister is prepared to pay them back until they get the first pension plan cheque. But we all know, Mr. Speaker, that they would have been better off if they had received unemployment insurance benefits to which they were entitled. They have won their case. It was more interesting than claiming under their retirement pension plan. In order to eliminate this inequity, last week I moved a motion under Standing Order 43. It was rejected by my friends opposite. I was asking the government to agree at least to pay the difference between the retirement pension plan and unemployment insurance benefits to which these people were entitled.
And I hope the minister will take that opportunity to correct the injustice towards those senior citizens for whom we as members of parliament must have the greatest respect considering their age and their services to society. Is it necessary to talk about it for 20 minutes? I hope not, Mr. Speaker, but I

think this is the most abominable action taken by a government against senior citizens. And I am sure that on the other side of this House some members agree with me and have already made recommendations to the minister to correct that unacceptable and indefensible injustice towards those senior citizens.
I do not know by what means I could defend that category of people, but as limited as they might be, I should not hesitate to insist that justice be rendered to those senior citizens manipulated by civil servants or by the government concerning a vested right. I find it absolutely scandalous that the government hesitates to correct completely an injustice. Of course, some people will tell me, that the situation will be partially corrected but we have no right to hesitate to correct completely a mistake made by civil servants and that the minister agreed to correct partially. The minister understands very well my view. If the minister has a minimum of human feelings, I think he can understand that those people are not only entitled to those allowances, but that they need them. I hope that those few comments and this appeal to the minister will be taken seriously and that eventually, and as soon as possible, the minister will announce, maybe tonight, that he will correct completely the injustice made by his own civil servants or his own department.
I also wish to mention that it might be important for the minister to consider a question that was put to me this morning, Mr. Speaker. I was asked if in the case of a person who normally would have been entitled to make a claim for unemployment insurance allowances and complying with all the criteria imposed by the minister, if the spouse could benefit from her husband's entitlement?
This has not been cleared up adequately. I have put this question to many persons who told me to put it to the minister since it seemed to bother him. It annoys me also but I believe that the government will respect the vested right of the widow whose husband was entitled to unemployment insurance benefits in 1976, regardless of the term, and will pay to her the benefits to which her husband was entitled.
Mr. Speaker, I will add also that the bill under study will probably annoy the farming community. In my riding as elsewhere in general, we know that there is a high manpower demand during the summer months. The claimant entitled to unemployment insurance benefits for a few months still will hesitate before accepting a summer job planting or harvesting if he is not guaranteed a minimum of eight weeks' work.
Obviously, the 12 week qualifying period will mean that thousands of claimants will be reluctant to work on farms next summer and they will possibly be called lazy but we must understand that if they do not work 12 weeks-and no farmer will want to guarantee them 12 weeks-they will surely not try to qualify for such employment next summer, since they are almost certain that it will be for only eight, nine or ten weeks. Such a situation not only prompts this type of worker to claim unemployment insurance but also annoys our farmers who do not have the help they need. They will lack workers and face enormous difficulties. I wonder whether we should not be
February 28, 1977

seriously considering other similar categories. It seems to me that farming already has enough problems and difficulties. After federal policies have hit the dairy industry, is this the time, Mr. Speaker, to impose new problems on our farmers?
I wonder whether serious consideration was given to the implications for our farmers and producers. It is my hope that at the committee stage, amendments will be put forward to avoid hindering more people, to make this legislation positive. 1 feel it is my duty as a-rpember to express these concerns, and as I said I am very much pleased that an hon. member opposite is worried by the bill and flatly stated he was not prepared to support it tonight. He hopes as we do that certain amendments may remedy the weaknesses. I will spare the House with data that were so aptly referred to by hon. members before me.
I commend the hon. member from Hamilton who stressed the need for an amendment in favour of areas now facing tremendous difficulties, and in my view the government cannot refuse to consider the amendment we will be putting forward. It is also my hope that the government, the minister in charge will remedy as fast as possible the injustice done to people 65 and over. This is the main item I wanted to bring to the attention of the House. I will conclude with the hope that the minister as I said will seriously consider my remarks as well as all remarks and recommendations that have been and will be put forward by my colleagues.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up the time of the House for long. I must say that the measures which the government has introduced to tighten up the unemployment insurance provisions are not necessarily measures I would oppose, given a different economic situation, given a different approach to the question of unemployment. But since we start this debate with unemployment at 8 per cent, perhaps 11 per cent in real terms, it seems to me the government continues to put the cart before the horse.
It is the duty of any government worth its salt to provide work for those of its citizens who wish to accept it. The present government and the government before it have failed appallingly in terms of their obligations to the citizens of this country. Let me say this: it is also the duty of all the citizens of this nation to accept work. I do not believe for one minute that we are a society capable of lying around in parks and dreaming while making this a worth-while community. If this House would accept a reciprocal ethic, one which says we have an obligation to provide work for the citizens, and that the citizens have an obligation to accept that work, we would not need this bill and we would not be sitting here arguing and worrying about the deficit in the unemployment insurance fund. We would then have a society which was starting to build together, a society with a common purpose. Therefore when I deal with the specific provisions of the bill I do not want to sound like a dog in the manger.
Employment and Immigration
I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that an NDP government does not like people cheating on unemployment insurance any more than anybody else does, and that we would be just as firm in making sure that the rules were obeyed. But I also want to tell you that in the constituency I represent, New Westminster, in one week in January 1,500 people showed up to get their unemployment insurance claims in. These were not people who were skiing out on Whistler or flying to Hawaii. They are not cheats. They are genuine, ordinary people, people this economy has failed. They want to do something productive. They do not want to sit around and loaf. To suggest they do, is a myth propagated by those who do not understand the nature of the Canadian people.
Not only did 1,500 people apply for unemployment insurance in my riding in one week in January, but in one trade alone, that of carpenter, 450 people registered as unemployed. No less than 450 carpenters, heads of families, were unemployed. Why? One of the reasons is that the OFY, LIP, Canada Works, Youth Works programs, you name them, are starting to take over some of the jobs they used to do, and instead of paying carpenters' rates they are paying lower rates for the same jobs.
Carpenters do not want to go on unemployment insurance. They want jobs. They are in the hiring halls every day but they are not called. They are not called because the government will not embark on capital projects to put them to work. We used to have a winter works program, not make-work, but real work. We could even now put our municipalities to work. I am pleased to hear the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) applauding. I know she agrees with this. We need capital works. I am looking at the minister now and hoping he will agree, too. We cannot continue to hold the fabric of Canadian society together with LIP. That doesn't work. We are not ready to sit in sloth in this country. We want meaningful capital investment.
If the minister would like to show some leadership I could take him to my riding; we could clear up the bars in my constituency along the Fraser River. It would take five years and thousands of people to do it. It would be creative in terms of people sitting on bars fishing. There is a whole recreation potential there which is fantastic. But we will not do it because an entrepreneur has not got up to say, "I want to do it." Mr. Speaker, if free enterprise refuses to do the things which create work, I believe there is an obligation upon the government to do so. But it has not done it, and it will not do it. I believe ministers will not do it because they are stultified. They refuse to See the other side of the equation.
We have to put people to work in order to reduce the crime rate and build this country back together. The crime rate is only one aspect of the social disintegration which has gone on as a result of the permissive society of the sixties. That society was not healthy, and the sooner the government recognizes it the better this country is going to be.
God knows, I would not stand in this House as a member of the New Democratic Party and object to unemployment insurance. Of course it is necessary, it is desirable, and it is humane.

February 28, 1977
Employment and Immigration
But a good government would not need very much unemployment insurance, and we would not be taking part in a raging debate over the subject if we had good government. We have experienced high unemployment because there has never been in this country a national government with a will to create full employment. I hope some day the people will wake up and vote for a government which has as its number one plank the creation of full employment. It can be done. It has been done in many societies, and it does not destroy the economy. It can even co-exist with free enterprise. But because chambers of commerce moan and groan we shall not move decisively in this direction.
Then again, we live in a society which is foreign-dominated, which means we cannot manufacture here; we simply dig out and ship, and until we come to grips with this aspect we shall not solve our unemployment problems.
Something that bothers me about this legislation, Mr. Speaker, is clauses 52 and 53, and I should just like to deal with specifics for a moment. As the minister knows, these provisions deal with experience rating. He has decided to abandon the principle of experience rating. My constituents who work in the mills are getting a little tired of having to subsidize other people. The guys who work all year long, apart from their three week holiday, and who do the tough job of pulling lumber off the chains, or who work in Oshawa manufacturing cars, are also getting a little tired of paying their unemployment insurance contributions knowing they will never collect. They would like to see their industries experience rated so that their premium is reduced. I think people in the construction industry, including my friends in the trades such as carpenters and plumbers, would be willing to see their industries experience rated as well. I think it is time we quit subsidizing contractors in Canada in that they have a ready made pool of labour available whenever they need it. It is a mistake to abandon experience rating. We should keep it in mind because it could make a significant difference in terms of the way we fund programs.
I said something about unemployment insurance cheaters. I want to give a commitment to the House that this party would be just as vigorous in prosecuting those who do not abide by the law. But I am a little tired of hearing about middle class families signing the weekly card for, say, a daughter in Hawaii, and then complaining about what a terrible society we live in. Honesty is for everybody, not just a few. One aspect to this life is that everybody wants to get as much as they can while giving as little as they have to, and that is wrong. I think we have all seen examples of the rare cheater on unemployment insurance, and the sympathetic mother who says, "Well, she has worked very hard and needs a holiday, and actually she would have taken a job if one had been available". We must prosecute people who cheat; otherwise the credibility of the whole unemployment insurance program will be brought into disrepute.

Having said that, I am still unsympathetic to the change from eight to 12 weeks. I have heard that it is proposed to move an amendment at some stage to the effect that 12 weeks is all right in some parts of the country, but there are areas where more than 12 weeks is all right too. This would not wash very well with someone in my riding who works eight weeks and cannot get unemployment insurance, and then he hears of someone in Nova Scotia who has worked eight weeks and can. If this House accepts that kind of amendment we will have lost our sense of proportion and justice. Any worker in British Columbia who works eight weeks is entitled to unemployment insurance every bit as much as someone in Nova Scotia or Newfoundland.

speechtext:
I would be happy to listen to the hon. member, who appears to be supporting the proposition that there is one law for one part of the country and another for another part. When a person is poor, he is just as poor in British Columbia as in Newfoundland. Poverty itself is a rotten thing, and those who are poor need help from this legislation, no matter in which part of the country they live, so let us not get sucked into the idea that because one part of the country has a higher unemployment rate than another part, the rules should be different in terms of collecting unemployment insurance. That would be a mistake. It would be divisive and would not contribute a darned thing to national unity.
I believe there are some obvious things that the government can do. The minister keeps shrugging his shoulders over what are remarkably practical propositions which have been made by members of this party and which, in effect, are supportive of the capital system. A tax cut at the lower income level would do a great deal to help small businesses in my community, but this has been rejected. A federal winter works program and additional housing programs have also been referred to by hon. members.
Then last, but I do not think least, cannot we somehow put the two major problems of increasing energy costs and unemployment together so as to reduce energy costs and create employment? What I have in mind is a national insulation program. Why in God's name this is rejected out of hand by the government is beyond my comprehension. There are six million building units in this country in need of insulation and of government financial assistance, yet the only move in this
February 28, 1977

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it certainly gives me great pleasure to rise to speak on this bill because I come from an area of Canada where the rate of unemployment is very high and where unemployment insurance is abused, and I will speak on the latter point later.
I have been dubbed here in the last two weeks as the $5 million constituency man, not only by people outside the House but by some members of the House and some cabinet members. 1 do not know whether they expect me to take my hat off to them, but let me point out that the estimated unemployment rate of 19.74 per cent in my area is underestimated because we have communities in northern Manitoba where the unemployment rate is running closer to about 90 per cent or 95 per cent.
Starting last fall we had a $1 million LIP allocation in the constituency. Before we could even snap our Fingers, another $1.4 million was made available through FLIP. Then of course on March 20 the Canada Works program was brought in. The First indication we had of the Canada Works program was on December 20. When the allocations were made, a total of $943,000 was made available through Canada Works. The Indian allocation amounted to $843,000, and the regular allocation was $100,000. I believe the reason that one allocation was made to Indians and a separate regular allocation was made is that whoever devised the Canada Works program had his head in the sand and did not realize what the implications would be. The money is all divided up by a ministerial advisory board which O.K.'s the project. I will tell you what it does.
It completely eliminates the Metis and the non-status Indians and the others, which is what we call white people in the north. This is consistent across all communities in the north. It drives a wedge between the community that has status Indians

February 28, 1977
Employment and Immigration
and the one that has non-status Indians and Metis. It divides these communities. The line is often through the bush. Often there is intermarriage and someone on the other side of the line is just as unemployed and just as deserving as the status Indians living on the reserve who will be getting the benefits.
I brought this to the attention of the minister because I thought there was no need for a ministerial advisory board to divide up something that has already been decided by the dreamers or the designers of this country in a program to which little thought was given. This program was thought up very quickly to give band-aid treatment to the problem of unemployment.
The next program that was brought out was Young Canada Works, with an allocation of $379,000 to the Churchill constituency. By this time whoever had designed the Canada Works program was at least smart enough not to make an Indian allocation and a regular allocation because they could see what would happen. They realized it would drive a wedge between the communities in the north. Next came the FLIP program. The FLIP program was for $1,088,000. Again this program was rushed into with little or no thought given to the allocation of moneys, and there was no planning of the projects that were to be carried out. In the course of about four months $2.4 million was allocated under LIP, $1,088,000 under FLIP, $943,000 under Canada Works, and now $379,000 under Young Canada Works. On top of this we have a program called LEAP which is also injecting money into the constituency.
I would not be surprised if the government were to come up with a "FLOP" program pretty soon. It would be called the federal labour optional program. The way the government is going the FLIP program and the "FLOP" program would fit in quite nicely, because the government is flip-flopping around the country trying to alleviate the unemployment situation. However, what it is really doing is thoroughly confusing people who are really in need of jobs.
What came along with the Canada Works program was a new batch of project officers. The project officers who worked in the LIP program were not even considered. Along came a whole new batch of project officers for each of these programs, and I will tell the House exactly what happened in the north. Some communities are 200 miles away from a central distribution point, and the only way to get to them is by air. One project officer was working on a LIP project, one on a FLIP project, and one on a Canada Works project. There were three different project officers who did not even know what the other project officers were doing. They were chartering aircraft into these communities to look after their part of the program, which is absolutely ridiculous. People in isolated areas of this country do not know whether their project officer is there for LIP, FLIP, Canada Works, or the LEAP program. They do not have any idea of what is going on.
One would think that with this much money going to the north there would be a saving on welfare payments I did some
(Mr. Smith (Churchill).J
checking into this, and I found that in communities living totally on welfare, even though several of these projects have been approved for them, the welfare is going to decrease by only 25 per cent.
Let us consider, for instance, the LIP program. Under the program there is a miniumum weekly wage of $167, from which deductions have to be made. In order for a family to survive it has to have its income supplemented, and this is where the welfare comes in. It seems that rather than one project officer looking after LIP and then somebody else coming in in connection with welfare to supplement incomes, it would be more reasonable to pay the person working on one of these make-work projects a decent salary so that he can keep his family in one of those isolated communities. This would cut down on the number of people spending money to travel into these communities, money which should be going to the communities.
I understand that for FLIP, LIP, Canada Works, LEAP and Young Canada Works, Manpower officers must make the referrals for jobs. It has been brought to my attention that the Manpower officers are just not capable of doing this job because they do not have the information required. They have a heavy workload as it is, and they do not have the confidence of the communities that they are capable of doing a good job of placing people in employment.
I will refer to a newspaper clipping which came out of the Winnipeg Free Press just last week. This story is from South Indian Lake. South Indian Lake is a typical northern community where unemployment is high. It is estimated 70 per cent of the residents are living on welfare-and an official from the community claims that ten people who collect unemployment insurance also collect welfare, even though they are working on one of these make-work projects. So what happens? The jobs with Manitoba Hydro on clearing projects which are available have not been filled. Six men were needed to harvest ice for next summer's fishing. These people could not be found in the community. No one wanted to go to work. People had to be brought in from outside in order to harvest the ice for next summer's operation.
The president of the local fishermen's association said that transport rates for fish to the Transcona plant went up to 8.5 cents a pound. There is a contract for five cents a pound, but because the trucks were not full the fishermen who were fishing were penalized. Meanwhile, 20 active fishermen make good money, and another 40 fishermen who are licensed are either back home working on one of the make-work projects, they are collecting UIC benefits, or they are partly on welfare. This is jeopardizing the entire fishery and penalizing fishermen who are out there trying to make a living at fishing.
The official said that the worst offender is the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, which is responsible for 60 per cent of the 650 residents who are treaty Indians. This is what is happening in most of the communities. There are only so many people in those communities. Everybody comes in with a new program, but what we should be looking for is one delivery system for these make-work pro-
February 28, 1977

grams. Why should we have four project officers spending thousands of dollars flying into one community to administer programs to try to give the people some benefit? The people at the other end are the losers because much is taken up in the administration of these programs. That money really is not getting to the people it should be reaching.
Canada Northlands is another good example. Even though money is going through Canada Northlands, the people are not benefiting from this program for the simple reason that the people who make the decisions are far removed from the needs of the communities, and they do not even know who is employed or who is not employed in these particular communities. The job creation branch is also involved in this. It is in charge of the project officers, and it also has to work very closely with Manpower, which is having a real problem because it is not able to look after the clients it now has in some communities.
1 would like to call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my request for an opportunity to elaborate on my question in the adjournment debate arises out of a question reported in Hansard of February 21 at page 3232 where 1 asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State (Mr. Guil-bault) for some explanation as to why the citizenship court in Simcoe is not able to process the many applications which came in as a result of the proclamation of the new Citizenship Act. The parliamentary secretary was at a bit of a disadvantage on that occasion. He was not aware of my question. He gave me the best answer possible under the circumstances, and I thank him for it. It was because he was not prepared to give
Adjournment Debate
a complete answer that 1 asked to be allowed to elaborate at this point.
Since that time the parliamentary secretary has communicated with the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts), who was kind enough to write a letter to me explaining this matter in greater detail. There are two paragraphs of the letter that I should like to read into the record:
My officials have investigated the points you raised and inform me that a slight delay did, in fact, occur in sending application forms under the new Citizenship Act to one or two county courts in Ontario. A telephone communication with the Simcoe county court on February 22, 1977. however, confirmed that the forms had been received on Friday, February 18, 1977.
On the matter of citizenship work currently being done by county courts, we have undertaken, at the request of the Ontario attorney general, a review of the situation. It is possible that as a result of this study the county courts may be relieved of their responsibilities . . .
That last is the sentence that concerns me, Mr. Speaker, and I will elaborate on the letter later in my remarks.
The predicament and confusion at Simcoe were disastrous, to say the least, to those people who came to make application for citizenship. The forms finally arrived a few days later, as has been indicated, but there was no letter appointing His Honour Judge John Pringle, the county court judge, to do the work in the citizenship court, nor the clerk of the county court to process the applications, so we are still without a citizenship court in the town of Simcoe. Their duties were terminated by a letter from the Registrar of Canadian Citizenship dated December 22, 1976, the relevant paragraph of which reads as follows:
Persons currently dealing with citizenship matters either in the judicial capacity or in the application taking function, will require new appointments. Further advice will be forwarded to you in this regard as soon as administrative details have been completed.
That advice still has not been received at the citizenship court in Simcoe. Over 100 people presented themselves at the court during the two or three weeks following the proclamation and, to say the least, there was frustration, as can be understood. The appointments of the judge, and of the clerk to take applications, still have not been made.
I have a letter here from the sheriff of Simcoe, and had a telephone conversation with his office this afternoon. In the letter he wrote:
The new appointments have not arrived to date and, therefore, the county court judge and the county court clerk are not authorized to accept applications.
This was confirmed, and the letter of appointment had not arrived by this afternoon. Mr. Speaker, how do we resolve this difficulty?
The county court clerk defines the problem as insufficient staff to take applications. He has to use the staff of the sheriffs office to do the work of the citizenship court for a federal department. He has been advised that a Mr. Peter Gale from the Hamilton citizenship office will be in Simcoe on Friday, March 18, from 8.30 a.m. to 4.30 p.m. to process applications. This would help take the workload off the sheriffs office, but it seems to me that help once a month is not

sufficient to handle the flow of applications in that area where there are a great many ethnic groups anxious to become Canadian citizens.
The county court judges in Simcoe and Gayuga do an excellent job in handling citizenships. Judge John Pringle in Simcoe and Judge Leach in Caledonia make the ceremony more than an examination and swearing in of the applicant. The Canadian flag and the provincial flag adorn the courtroom. The band from the local high school leads singing of our National Anthem and God Save the Queen. A welcome committee made up of prominent citizens in the community and members of the RCMP attend a reception sponsored by the Imperial Order of the Daughters of the Empire where the new citizens are welcomed. This is a truly impressive and meaningful ceremony, and I would be concerned if it were not maintained.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to refer to an article in the Simcoe Reformer. The judge told the newspaper's correspondent that he viewed the occasion with a little nostalgia, and feared some of the meaning of the old ceremony may be lost when the new Citizenship Act goes into effect this Tuesday.
