subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-LEGAL AUTHORITY OF DEPARTMENT TO REMOVE CHILDREN FROM CUSTODY OF PARENTS-SUGGESTED COMPLIANCE WITH PROVINCIAL LAW

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-LEGAL AUTHORITY OF DEPARTMENT TO REMOVE CHILDREN FROM CUSTODY OF PARENTS-SUGGESTED COMPLIANCE WITH PROVINCIAL LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my purpose in rising this evening is to attempt to obtain further information from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Penner).
My intervention is the result of a question I asked on January 31 with respect to something almost incredible which happened in Saskatchewan. I was referring to children living on reserves in that province, children who had apparently been apprehended by departmental officials without legal authority, as the minister admitted when answering my question on January 31.1 asked the question originally because some 700 children apparently have been apprehended by the department, and I felt that the matter affects a substantial number of children who may have been apprehended without legal or judicial assessment as to whether the apprehension was justified.
When replying the minister indicated to me that that particular action had been taken because a number of sad situations with respect to children obtained on the reserves. But I think that answer was not sufficient to meet the point of principle which I raised when I questioned the minister on January 31.
What has happened has not merely happened in the recent past. The matter has been of concern for the department for some years, apparently. According to my information some of these apprehensions took place over five years ago, when children were taken from their parents without a court order. They have been placed in foster homes, or reared in foster homes, for a number of years. I simply point out to the parliamentary secretary, who is a compassionate and sensitive person, the wrench that could take place where it is determined that the parents have the right to have their children back. These children may have accepted the foster parents as the actual parents and accepted the other children of the family as their brothers and sisters.
That is only one side of the matter. An even more important side is the right of parents in this country who have any agency, whether government or otherwise, take children from them without judicial review.
I suppose the answer the parliamentary secretary will give tonight is that there is no agreement between the province of Saskatchewan and the federal government. I realize we have a possible conflict in the sense of jurisdictional authority with respect to Indian children. However, it causes me a great deal of concern that over a period of some years, at least five years as far as I am able to determine, the provincial government and federal government have been haggling over who will pay the expense with regard to the administration of child apprehension on Indian reserves in the province of Saskatchewan.
I find it incredible that we have two levels of government haggling over the cost of this. The great social concern here is
February 28, 1977

being ignored and being left to the rather arbitrary and, in fact, unlawful actions on the part of the department. It is a very basic principle of our law in Canada that as far as the taking of children is concerned in any province one cares to look at, the parents have a right to have a court review the circumstances and give an independent assessment as to whether the apprehension is justified.
The department in effect has been guilty of some acts of malfeasance in the cases to which I referred. I am concerned because we have these 700 cases. If they have been taken without a court review or without any application to the courts, we might have a situation where these 700 children may be ordered to go back to their parents or be left in a state of limbo.
I would like the parliamentary secretary to state this evening what precise action the department is going to take with regard to this sad and tragic situation. 1 say this on behalf of the parents who have possibly had their children taken wrongfully. I say it on behalf of the foster parents who may have received children and regard them as their own, with the children regarding the foster parents as their new parents. There will be an awful wrench if it is found to be an illegal seizure on the part of the departmental officials.
1 ask the parliamentary secretary to tell us this evening if the department has any game plan with respect to this whole problem because there are many people concerned about this from the point of view of the rights of individuals. There are many immediate practical situations which we have before us. At least 700 beg some satisfactory answer from the department. 1 will be interested in hearing the response tonight.

speakeroldname: Mr. B. Keith Penner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-LEGAL AUTHORITY OF DEPARTMENT TO REMOVE CHILDREN FROM CUSTODY OF PARENTS-SUGGESTED COMPLIANCE WITH PROVINCIAL LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) has raised this question because the department has a very satisfactory answer. It is a good opportunity for me to elaborate this evening on the concern which has been so well expressed by the hon. member.
The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development pays full costs for maintenance of 778 Indian children in Saskatchewan who have been taken into care by the Provincial Superintendent of Child Welfare as a result of court action. Departmental staff and employees of band councils have arranged foster homes for an additional 607 children, also maintained at departmental expense. The hon. member will see immediately that there is no question at all about haggling over costs, as he suggested. In such cases, the child's parents have given consent for the arrangements, except in instances where we have been unable to trace or contact them.
When we are called in to help a child who has been abandoned, neglected or abused, we first try to locate the parents. If the parents are available, every attempt is made to help them improve the situation. However, if the parents wish to have the child cared for in a foster home, the best possible placement is arranged with their approval. I am advised that in
Adjournment Debate
a good many cases attempts to obtain provincial participation are fruitless.
When the parents of a child in need cannot be contacted, or when they refuse to take responsibility for the child's proper care, assistance is sought from the provincial department of social services or from the RCMP, since they alone have the authority to take custody of a child, or to take the matter to the appropriate court. When the province and the RCMP refuse to act, we are faced with a critical moral and human problem, and have no alternative but to make the best possible arrangements for the child.
It must be obvious to any honestly concerned observer that there is nothing illegal in arranging for foster homes when the child's parents consent to it. There is a very great difference between breaking the law and having no law under which to act. For many years, parents who needed such services depended upon the department to provide them. It would be unjust to deprive them or their children of this sort of care until such time as better arrangements can be made. There is no question of the rights of either the children or their parents being ignored, and there is no evidence that the arrangements that have been made for the children are unsatisfactory. Any parent who is dissatisfied can have their child returned at any time. I would hope, however, that any such decision would be made with care, and in the knowledge of its implications.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-PROPOSED RESEARCH CENTRE AT WINNIPEG-DELAY IN COMPLETING LAND PURCHASE AGREEMENT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
NATIONAL DEFENCE-PROPOSED RESEARCH CENTRE AT WINNIPEG-DELAY IN COMPLETING LAND PURCHASE AGREEMENT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 23 I asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) to tell us what the intentions of the government were with regard to the defence research centre for Winnipeg which was announced three years ago. Since that announcement the city of Winnipeg has been subject to an undue amount of procrastination and stalling tactics from the Liberal government here in Ottawa. This has cost Winnipeg a considerable amount in lost revenue and placed an unnecessary burden on the taxpayers of that city. 1 am referring in particular to the 111 acres of land on which the defence research centre is supposed to be constructed.
When one takes a look at the record of government in connection with the research centre one cannot but seriously question its motives. Is the government so unconcerned about declining Liberal popularity in western Canada that it is deciding to write off western Canada altogether, or is it sheer confusion and disorganization which have caused delay in the construction of the centre?
I think it worth noting that ever since the former minister of defence, the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson) made the announcement in February, 1974, that Winnipeg would be receiving a defence research base, nothing has happened in terms of action by Ottawa. For the record I would point out that on October 22, 1976, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Dionne) stated in response to a question I put to him:

February 28, 1977
Adjournment Debate
I am pleased to inform the hon. member that the new research establishment in Manitoba will be constructed in his constituency.
I wonder if that is still the intention of the government, because on February 18 the Minister of National Defence told us that the defence research centre project had been deferred for a period of between six months and a year. In the face of these conflicting and confusing statements, I contend that the government has a moral obligation to come clean with the city of Winnipeg and make a clear cut statement as to whether or not it really intends to purchase the land and build a centre. It is interesting to note that the 1977-78 estimates for national defence make provision for an expenditure of over $20 million for a defence research establishment in Manitoba, yet the government will not even tell us where in Manitoba it will be constructed or when the work will begin.
The government should be more responsive to the city of Winnipeg because there are a number of crucial matters at stake. First of all, Mr. Speaker, there is the matter of 111 acres of prime land that was originally negotiated to be sold at a price of $1,200,000 to the federal government. During the time the Liberal government has wasted in stalling, the value of this land has increased three times. The federal government in all fairness to the people of Winnipeg should renegotiate this deal so that the taxpayers of Winnipeg will not be the losers.
The second matter is that if the federal government does not intend to use this particular parcel of land it should notify the city of Winnipeg so that consideration might be given to using it for other purposes. As I say, this is one of the last prime pieces of residential land in the city.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the federal government should not place a burden on Winnipeg taxpayers by not paying any taxes on this land. It should take the immediate steps necessary to reimburse the city of Winnipeg for the lost revenue on this land that it could have been collecting from private developers.
During the past three years there have been numerous communications between the city of Winnipeg and the federal government. Let us take a look at the number of communications since the fall of 1976. In each instance I must point out that the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Guay), better known as the minister of nothing, has been aware of these communications, yet he has seen fit to do nothing. As I said, let us take a chronological look at the events since the fall of 1976.
On September 13 last a letter was sent to the Department of Justice from the city of Winnipeg enclosing a draft agreement. On September 21 an acknowledgement was received. On October 26 a re-draft of the agreement was received by the city of Winnipeg from the Department of Justice. On November 8 a letter was sent to the Department of Justice on changes to the agreement. On November 24 a letter was received by the city of Winnipeg on the price. On November 26 a memo was sent to the land surveys and real estate department of Winnipeg on discussions of price. On December 27 a letter was sent to the Department of Justice outlining changes to the agreement. On January 13, 1977, a letter from the Department of Justice advised that material was forwarded to Ottawa for consideration.
These, Mr. Speaker, are just a few instances of the constant communications going on over a project that was announced three years ago. What has the minister of nothing from St. Boniface been doing in the past few months to assist this project? The answer is quite simply, nothing. That is why he is called the minister of nothing and I suppose he is paid to do nothing. In the meantime the city of Winnipeg suffers.
In all sincerity, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that the national defence research centre should become a political football. Either the Liberal government is serious in its commitment or it is not. When the. Minister of National Defence told me on February 23 that he did not expect the city of Winnipeg to hold on to the land, what did the minister of nothing do? Absolutely nothing. During all of these deliberations the hon. member has done nothing whatsoever to help resolve this matter. He did not even make the effort to communicate with the city of Winnipeg.
As I pointed out earlier, the 1977-78 estimates for national defence include a defence research establishment for Manitoba and I, along with many other residents of the city of Winnipeg, would like to know where and when the government intends to build this research station. After all, Mr. Speaker, surely to heaven the Minister of National Defence must have some idea as to the future of this project, especially if officials from his department have it included in the 1977-78 estimates. I really do not think it is fair to the people of Winnipeg to ask them to put up with this procrastination.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-PROPOSED RESEARCH CENTRE AT WINNIPEG-DELAY IN COMPLETING LAND PURCHASE AGREEMENT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should know that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) has stated in this House that the project to create a new defence research establishment at Winnipeg is in temporary suspension. The primary reason for that is that the Minister of National Defence wishes to study the rationalization of the scientific, research and industrial processes in the Department of National Defence in relation to other industrial efforts.
The minister has stated:
I think we want to look for things which will serve the best long-term interests of Winnipeg and all of western Canada and also to rationalize our defence purchasing so that it is to the best advantage of Canadian industry and the armed forces.
I am advised by the DND that no land deals have been concluded with the city of Winnipeg for the proposed site of the research establishment. Would the hon. member not be the first to chastise the government for paying taxes or grants in lieu of taxes on property that it did not own? It would seem to me that the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) has enough talent and ability to defend himself, and I would leave it to him. He must be something more than the "minister for nothing" because he must have done something to get under the hon. member's skin.
